Memorandum recd. from Shri Praveen More, All India Forum of
Forest Movements (AIFFM)
The Compensatory Afforestation Fund Bill, 2015, seeks to provide a statutory framework for using
the funds collected from user agencies seeking diversion of forest land for non-forest purposes for
"compensatory afforestation", "net present value" and related activities. In order to understand this Bill,
it is important to understand the legal background to this issue, which is summarised below.
Background- What Are Compensatory Afforestation and Net Present Value?
Under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, a law enacted for protection of forests, no "forest
land" can be used for any non-forest purpose without the permission of the Central government. Such
permission is referred to as "diversion" of the said forest land. Upon such diversion, the Forest
(Conservation) Rules require that either twice the area of diverted land of 'degraded forest' or the same
area of non-forest land be set aside for. "compensatory af forestation" — essentially tree plantations. The
user agency is required to pay sufficient funds for such planting to the State government, which is then
required to do the planting.
In 2002 and subsequently, over a period of several years, in the course of hearing the Godavarman
case
1, the Supreme Court issued a series of orders that changed this system. In response to concerns
that compensatory afforestation was not taking place, the court ordered that:
• Henceforth, the funds for compensatory afforestation would be deposited not with the State
governments, but in a specialised central fund;
• This fund would be administered by a central body called the Compensatory Afforestation
Management and Planning Authority;
• Payments would include not only money for various categories of compensatory afforestation,
but also for the "Net Present Value" of the forest being destroyed - calculated as per an
arbitrary figure of Rs 5.8 - 9.6 lakhs per hectare.
The said Authority was notified by the Central government but given no statutory basis. As a result
these funds are now lying unspent, up to a total of over Rs 38,000 crores.
Problems with the Current System
There are some severe problems with the system of compensatory afforestation and net present
value payments as it is currently instituted. These have been made more acute due to the Bill contravening
the legal requirements of the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of
Forest Rights Act), 2006 (FRA for short) unanimously passed by Parliament after the Supreme Court's
order of 2002 creating this special fund. The current Bill not only does not address these problems, but
will make them much worse. The problems include:
• Depriving people of their rights over forests and forest land. A forest is a source of
minor forest produce like fruits, food items, saleable tendu patta or kendu patta, fuelwood,
102
1 WP 202/95, T.N. Godavarman Thirumalpad and Ors. vs. Union of India and Ors.

103
medicinal herbs, etc., as well as containing water bodies, grazing areas, common lands and
other areas that people depend on for their livelihood. Even where people in fact own the
so-called "forest land" (a lot of which has never been legally notified), as in community
lands in the hill areas of Manipur, they are paid, nothing for its diversion.  Destruction of
the forest deprives adivasis, forest dwellers and other local communities of some or all of
their livelihood or basic resources– for which they are neither informed, nor consulted, nor
compensated. Enactment of the FRA now makes it illegal to remove forest dwellers from
forest land till the process of recognition of their forest rights has been completed. In the
Niyamgiri case, the Supreme Court has upheld the FRA's requirement that the gram sabha
must decide whether their forest land may be diverted. Despite this, forest diversion, often
based on obtaining fraudulent gram sabha resolutions, is continuing.
• Equating tree planting with compensating the loss of diverse natural forests, The system
implies that, if an equivalent area of land is planted with trees, it is somehow equivalent to
the environmental damage caused by destroying an area of natural forest. In fact a natural
forest has multiple environmental and cultural values - such as providing forest products
and ecosystem services including water, a habitat for wildlife,, biodiversity, abode of deities,
etc. These cannot be recreated simply by planting trees in another location, often faraway
from the site of forest destruction.
• Encouraging financial malpractices: The present Bill, in its preamble part, cites absence
of institutional mechanism as a reason for huge unspent funds in ad hoc CAMPA and hence
tries to make a case for the current Bill. However, this does not stand scrutiny. The 2013
CAG (Comptroller Auditor General, India) report on Compensatory Afforestation and CAMPA
rightly pointed out that even in cases where state forest departments had money for
plantation, not much could be shown on the ground as activities really undertaken. Instead,
CAMPA funds have been used for highly questionable manner. Recent reports in Times of
India and Economic Times
2. citing a monitoring report prepared by Maharasthra State
Forest Department, and other sources reiterate that most of the compensatory plantations
shown on paper do not exist and funds earmarked for compensatory afforestation are being
arbitrarily spent on other activities. Independent studies conducted by civil society organizations
in 2013-14, also bear this out.
• Encouraging seizure of community and individual lands for plantation purposes. In most
cases, non-forest land used for such plantations consists of customary community or
individual lands of adivasis and forest communities on which their rights have not been
recognized, and over which forest department has administrative or legal control.

articleshow/47239889.cms, see also: http://articles.economictimes.indiatimes.com/2015-03-24/news/60439177_1_campa-
guidelines-forest-land-campa-funds

Even where so called 'degraded forest' land is used for compensatory afforestation, the FRA
requires prior completion of the recognition of forest rights in these areas, and where the
land is claimed/pereceived as community forest resources (CFRs) by Gram Sabha, according
to the provisions of the FRA the gram sabha is the proper legal authority for its management.
Neither the forest department nor the State or Central Government have the right to
undertake compensatory afforestation on CFRs or other common lands without the gram
sabha's consent. Seizure of land for compensatory afforestation thus leads to double
displacement of communities from their livelihood resources, the first time for diversion of
forest land and the second time for compensatory afforestation.
• Levying of monetary charges does not compensate for the resulting environmental
and livelihood damage. This approach assumes that, just by requiring companies or the
government to pay money for forest destruction, environmental damage will be contained.
This ignores the multi-faceted impacts and nature of environmental damage caused by
natural forest destruction which are closely inter linked with damaged lives and livelihoods.
What is needed is a system of environmental regulation that will protect people's interests
and the forests in a democratic and transparent manner. The current Bill
does not achieve this in any sense.

General Observations
The Bill Threatens the Rights of Adivasis and Other Forest Dwellers
As stated above, the most fundamental flaw with the current system is that those most directly
affected by forest destruction - adivasis and forest communities - have no control whatsoever over the
process. The current Bill will make this even worse, as despite enactment of the Forest Rights Act, 2006,
it neither refers to the Act nor the rights of forest dwelling communities (redundant)
This will neither result in any reduction of forest destruction nor in any just spending of this
money. Indeed, the Supreme Court's own expert committee on Net Present Value, the Kanchan Chopra
Committee, had recommended in May 2006 that NPV should be shared as per a tripartite sharing
formula. The formula granted the majority share of NPV money to local bodies and State governments.
Plantations by the forest department have become one of the biggest threats to the lands of
adivasis and forest dwellers - especially with regard to land used for shifting cultivation and other
common lands resulting in frequent conflicts. There is no provision for the local community to have any
voice in deciding where this plantation will take place.

thus violates the spirit and letter of the Forest Rights Act, 2006 as well as of the Panchayats (Extension
to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA for short) and will encourage further seizure of community lands.

110
Further, the Bill Will Legalise an Environmentally Destructive and Ill-Thought Tree Plantation Programme
without any consideration of how the resulting changes in land use will impact local livelihoods.
Little difference between the present Bill and the ad hoc CAMPA
The STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS appended to the bill repeatedly mentions the
CAG's observations about Compensatory afforestation and ad-hoc CAMPA, claiming that the present bill
has been framed keeping them in mind :
The Comptroller and Auditor General in its report on Compensatory afforestation in India (21 of
2013) observed that given the substantial amounts of funds being collected under the compensatory
afforestation, the expenditure there from, the overall objectives of conservation, protection, regeneration
and management of forests, conservation, protection and management of wild life and its habitats and
compensatory afforestation; the clear public purpose involved in the work relating to CAMPA, "there is
need, to review the existing paradigm of CAMPA ". "The Comptroller and Auditor General recommended
that this should be done in a way that enhances transparency, brings CAMP A within the broader focus
of both Parliament and State Legislatures and in greater public view so as to ensure the largest possible
stakeholders' participation. italis added)
The present bill apparently is not creating anything substantially different from ad-Hoc CAMPA,
other than providing that state forest departments will have almost total control over the huge fund
already lying with the ad hoc CAMPA, and the new money that will be deposited. However, it is the
failure of this very arrangement which had led to the Supreme Court creating the ad hoc CAMPA in the
first place. Instead of making the exercise more transparent and increasing public oversight, the bill
essentially takes the fund and its disbursement away from judicial scrutiny and re-legitimizes the same
institutional structure which provides room for more corruption and financial irregularities. It also
empowers the state forest departments and Ministry of Environment, forests and Climate Change to
utilize the funds for any other purpose they deem fit, while totally excluding the forest dwelling communities
who lose the most when their customary forests are diverted from any say in the matter. This is in total
violation of the Forest Rights Act and PESA and the rights and authority vested in gram sabhas to protect,
conserve and manage their community forest resources. The decision making control over utilization of
the Funds needs to be in the hands of those communities who are being dispossessed, and through their
direct agencies. The same holds true for demarcation and regeneration of the common lands to be taken
up for compensatory afforestation. By vesting control over the funds in the powerful forest bureaucracy
the Bill will facilitate a scenario of yet more injustice and rights denial at the grassroots. It will obstruct
the implementation of FRA and PESA.
More importantly, the state forest officers will see this as a direct incentive to promote and
expedite forest diversion—the red tape and jurisdictional ambiguities over ad-Hoc Campa funds have
hindered large-scale tinkering with the funds so far. In the present scenario, the CAMPA bill will
smoothen forest officials' unimpeded access to those funds without adequate safegaurds.

111
The Bill stands on legally as well as scientifically questionable premises, excludes most of the stakeholders
whose concurrence in both forest diversion and raising new plantations have now been mandated by law
(FRA and PESA), and allows for a top-down bureaucratic practice.
The Bill, in its present form, must be scrapped.

There is undoubtedly a need for a statute on this issue, if only to remedy the situation created by
the Supreme Court's orders. But this Bill will not achieve this objective. Rather, the new statute should
consider the following elements and the drafting of the bill must be informed by those
• The Re-drafting of the Bill must be preceded by a review by an impartial and transparently
constituted team of environmental experts and representatives of civil society groups to look
into the CA process so far, including a thorough ground-level fact-finding exercise to
determine how CA is being executed in the areas where deforestation (forest diversion)
events are taking place: in particular, the review should look into the question of land for
CA, and present as well as potential impacts on communities, and specific instances of
violation of laws and denial of justice as well as issues of non-compliance and alleged
corrupt practices.
• A complete overhaul of the Forest Clearance mechanism is called for before such a statute
comes into being or even considered : instead of facilitating fast-track clearance of
development projects that cause deforestation and displace forest communities, it should re
really an environmental instrument: each proposed case of forest diversion, beyond those
specifically recommended by Gram Sabhas under relevant provisions of FRA should be
looked into separately, and judged only by its potential environmental impacts at micro-level
as well as the larger ecological landscape level. Gram Sabha consent for all kinds of forest
diversion projects are already legally mandatory and the new FC mechanism should incorporate
this by making necessary changes in the FC(Rules) itself. The Rules should be changed in
consonance with the relevant provisions of FRA and PESA, the GO issued by MoEF in
august 2009, and the verdict of the Supreme Course in the Niyamagiri-Vedanta case in April
2013, all of which reiterate the primacy of Gram Sabhas in decision making.
• The manifestly failed process of Compensatory Afforestation must be generally done away
with. Because these plantations, instead of ensuring environmental compliance, only facilitate
and escalate deforestation, allow a wide margin for corrupt practices, and finally encroach
upon people's lands and forests, the Forest Clearance mechanism should not generally have
this provision at all.
• In exceptional cases, and only if the concerned communities give prior informed consent,
the plantation part of CA should be handed over to affected communities: who should
identify suitable land, species and cost for such plantations independent of interference by
forest department or user agency. For this purpose, degraded forest land as well as plantation

112
areas with commercial monoculture (eucalyptus, teak, pine varieties) can be used. Under
no circumstances, community-held Jhum/podu areas with 40 percent canopy density (and
below), can be used for Compensatory Afforestation.
• In case a community gives its consent to a particular case of forest diversion, its control,
access and use of forests must figure prominently in determining the mitigation exercise,
irrespective of whether such control, access and usage have been officially recorded by
forest department. Section 5 of FRA provides for community control and access of all kinds
of forests, and Section 3 and 4 of the same act stipulate that rights of governance control,
access and usage have already vested in forest communities.

manner. The communities who had been displaced or in any affected by cases of approved

including development of various sustainable forest-based livelihood programmes inc: the

Protection Act.

Memorandum received from Shri Kumar Anirvan and others
At the outset, we seek condonation of delay, if any, in submitting our views. However we hope:
you will take them info consideration during the deliberations of the committee, to examine the CAF Bill,
2015.
We, the undersigned, strongly believe that the CAF Bill 2015 in its present form will not able to
the ecological security of this country, but is far more likely to (a) result in ecological disaster, and (b)
foster massive corruption in the forestry sector. Expert views on this subject have recently appeared in
The Hindu (Sowing the Seeds of a Disaster, July 29, 2015) and other media articles.
Here we present some well-founded reasons why the Bill must be recast on the basis of sound
science and commonsense. We also show how the Compensatory Afforestation Management Planning
Authority (CAMPA) corpus can be utilized to genuinely benefit the country.
1. Flawed premise: The Bill is fundamentally flawed in that it assumes that the loss of forests
or other natural habitats as a result of development projects can be 'compensated' by simply
planting trees elsewhere. The truth is, forests and other natural habitats are extremely
complex ecosystems that have evolved to a state of ecological equilibrium over millions of
years, with their full complement of pollinators, seed dispersers, predators and prey. These
natural habitats are the repositories of India's extraordinarily rich biodiversity, which is
already under tremendous stress. The 'compensatory afforestation' that this country has
witnessed so far predominantly consists of raising artificial plantations of non-native species
of trees, which have zero biodiversity value. Even where plantations of mixed species of
native trees have been raised, they do not come anywhere close to replicating the natural
habitat that was destroyed.
2. Tree planting is no panacea: It is also meaningless to plant trees in lieu of diverted natural
habitats such as wetlands or grasslands, which have their own distinct ecological value.
Sometimes, over-zealous tree planting in the wrong place can badly affect a natural ecosystem.
Here is just one example of how the compensatory afforestation approach often ends, up
not just being a 'greenwash', but an ecological disaster as well. From 1980 to 2005, the
Kudremukh Iron Ore Company Limited (KIOCL) strip-mined hill slopes clothed in virgin
rainforests in the heart of Karnatakas Kudremukh National Park. Besides this horrendous
damage to the fragile ecosystem, over 150 million tonnes of tailings - the waste mud left
over after extraction of low grade ore - were dumped into a pristine, 100 metre deep,
forested valley. To 'compensate' for this loss of natural habitats, KIOCL went on a massive
compensatory afforestation spree, planting millions of trees. The problem with this was
twofold: the trees were non-native species; and they were planted on adjoining areas of
natural grassland, which are an extremely important component of the Bhadra River's
Watershed. Thus, apart from the forested hill slopes and the valley that were destroyed by
mining activities, a third natural habitat, in the form of ecologically important grasslands,
115

116
was destroyed through mindless tree planting. The CAF Bill 2015, if approved in its current
form, would end up repeating such colossal mistakes all over the country.
3. Nothing but a fig leaf: 'Compensatory afforestation' is nothing but a fig leaf to cover up
the diversion of natural habitats in the name of development. It is a sad irony that the money
spent and the plantations raised are then touted as 'achievements' towards a 'Green India'.
4. Abysmal record: Afforestation in general has had an abysmal record in India. Massive
amounts of money have been spent with little to show on the ground. In Maharashtra, a
recent official evaluation of ten-year old plantations in all 11 Forest Circles has shown that
74% of plantations have failed. 13% were shown to be partially successful and only 13%
were deemed successful. Under the 12th Plan, an allocation of 2500 crore rupees was made
for the National Afforestation Programme, but with little to show for it. The Parliamentary
Standing Committee on Science & Technology and Environment & Forests in 2015 has
recorded that despite massive budgetary provisions, 40% of forests in the country are still
degraded. 'Compensatory Afforestation' has had an even more dismal record, with numerous
instances of money allotted for afforestation being misused for purchasing vehicles and
installing air conditioners. According to some studies, Goa used 69% of its compensatory
afforestation allocation on buildings, vehicles and computers. Similarly, Andhra Pradesh
wanted to spend 43% on construction activities, Sikkim 53%, Himachal Pradesh 53% and
Tamil Nadu 67%.
5. The CAMPA corpus must not be squandered: It would be an immense tragedy if the huge
corpus of over 35,000 crore rupees that has accrued with CAMPA is frittered away on
meaningless and corruption-ridden tree planting schemes. Even setting aside the flawed
premise that 'compensatory afforestation' is based upon, analysis shows that non-forestland
is virtually unavailable for afforestation. In it's report of September 2013 on compensatory
afforestation, the CAG has put forth some startling facts. It computes that between 2006
and 2012, state environment departments were to get 103,382 hectares of non-forestland
for afforestation from revenue departments. Instead, all they got was 28,086 hectares, out
of which afforestation was carried out on "an abysmal 7,280.84 hectare constituting seven
percent of the land which ought to have been received".
6. Other funds available for afforestation: Currently, Japan International Co-operation Agency
(JICA) has committed 15,000 crore rupees for 22 forestry projects in 13 States. Other
multi-lateral agencies have committed huge sums of money for afforestation in the past and
will doubtless do so in the future. This obviates the need for CAMPA funds to be used for
the same endeavour.
7. How CAMPA funds can be used to truly benefit the nation: The massive corpus
accrued under CAMPA is akin to 'blood money' collected from, the destruction offorests

117
and other natural habitats. Squandering this fund would only add insult to injury. Instead
of spending this sovereign fund on highly leakage-prone tree planting projects, we suggest
that it would be better spent in the following way:
• Defragmentation of large forest blocks: When ill-planned development projects are
thrust into the heart of PAs, the result is fragmentation, i.e., the breaking up of large
forest blocks into smaller and more vulnerable patches. Peer reviewed scientific
research has clearly established that fragmentation is one of the most serious threats
to long-term biodiversity conservation, causing several devastating impacts; among
other things, it disrupts landscape connectivity, affecting dispersal of animals, and
creates new edges that expose forests to exploitation and severe degradation. The Bill
must be modified to allow a major percentage of CAMPA funds to be utilized for
defragmenting and consolidation of the remaining large blocks of natural old-growth
forests. Among other measures, this could involve (i) Strategic land acquisitions (ii)
Extinguishment of old leased lands in thickly forested areas (iii) Voluntary resettlement
of people from PAs (iv) Creation of wildlife corridors, and (v) Facilitating natural
regeneration of degraded forests. CAMPA, being our sovereign fund, is the only one
available for such ecologically vital activities, which are not allowed by international
agencies funding afforestation projects in India.
• Mitigation of the impacts of development projects in and around PAs: all
development projects within and in the vicinity of PAs will inevitably result in a
multitude of negative impacts. Some, if not all, of these impacts could be mitigated
to an extent through scientifically designed measures. For instance, where a highway
running through a PA is to be widened from a two lane one to a four lane or six lane
one, it will become impossible for animals to cross the road safely from one side of
the forest to the other. Often, the NHAI claims lack of funds for effective mitigation.
CAMPA funds would be invaluable in such cases for re-establishing habitat connectivity
through the careful deployment of traffic overpasses and wildlife underpasses at
critical animal crossing points.
• Assisting natural regeneration of degraded forests on the basis of good science:
the other important activity that needs to be funded through CAMPA is natural
restoration or regeneration of degraded forests. The approach here must be to first
identify degraded forest areas with existent rootstock, and invest only on appropriate
protection measures such as trenching, fencing and fire prevention. The degraded
forests will then recover through a natural process at a very nominal cost to the
exchequer. Funding for artificial plantations should only be considered in extremely
degraded areas with no existing rootstock.

118
We are at a critical moment in India's fight to achieve ecological security while ensuring economic
and social progress. If the CAF Bill 2015 is recast on the basis of sound science, it can create the
foundation for a far-sighted, and genuinely beneficial strategy to protect India's forests. If not, it may
result in the squandering of thirty five thousand crore rupees on corruption-ridden 'afforestation' projects
involving digging pits, buying polythene bags for raising saplings, and planting trees that can never
become forests.
We humbly request the honourable Rajya Sabha Standing Committee to take these matters into
careful consideration while providing recommendations on the CAF Bill 2015.

Sub: Compensatory Afforestation Fund Bill, 2015.
The Compensatory Afforestation Fund Bill, 2015 introduced in Lok Sabha on 8th May 2015, is
a right effort by the MoEF & CC in the direction of ensuring speedy and timely utilization of funds kept
with Adhoc CAMPA. We have following suggestions on the Bill:-
(i) The Bill provides that out of all the compensatory funds deposited by the User Agencies,
the State Authority (CAMPA) will retain 90% and the remaining 10% will be transferred to
the National Authority (CAMPA). Except Net Present Value (NPV), rest of the funds deposited
by the User Agencies are meant for site specific works. Any curtailment will seriously
hamper the proposed site specific works. Hence, it is proposed that 10% of the funds,
deposited under the NPV head, only be transferred to the National Authority. [Reference-
Section 3(4)]
(ii) The Bill also provides that the aforesaid 90% of the fund, retained by the State Authority,
can be used every year only after approval of the Annual Plan of Operations (APO) by the
National Authority. This translates into de facto control of all the funds by the National
Authority. This provision is against the spirit of the Bill [Reference-Section 15(1) (i)].
Instead, the National Authority may issue detailed guidelines on allocation limits to various
sectors, prohibition of certain activities, etc. The National Authority may also put in place
a strong monitoring and evaluation system to ensure compliance of the guidelines.
(iii) The Bill provides for formation of the State Authority consisting of Governing Body, Steering
Committee and Executive Committee. Governing Body is proposed to be headed by the
Honorable Chief Minister. Considering the busy schedule of the Honorable Chief Minister,
it is proposed that the Governing Body of the State Authority may be headed by the
Honorable Forest Minister of the state. [Reference-Section 10]
(iv) The Bill gives Rule making powers to Central Government. Various site specific projects,
for which funds are deposited by the User Agencies, will be implemented in the specific
state only, further more, there are many provisions relating to establishment of state fund,
its management and constitution of Governing Body and other Committees. My suggestion
is that considering different situations in different states, the rule making powers be given
to the State Governments. [Reference Section 30]

REPORT
INTRODUCTION
The Department of Biotechnology was initially set up as an Independent Board in 1982 and thereafter
became a full fledged Department under the Ministry of Science and Technology in 1986. The main
mandate of the Department is:
(i) To evolve policies and integrated programmes in biotechnology and ensure their implementation
and monitoring.
(ii) To identify specific programmes of Research and Development and manufacturing in biologicals
and biotechnology and oversee the initiation and pursuit of related research and manufacturing
activities.
(iii) To identify, set up and support Centres of Excellence for Research and Development in
biotechnology and ensure proper dovetailing of their activities as per national priorities and
objectives.
(iv) To act as a screening, advising and approving agent of the Government with regard to import
and transfer of new technologies for the manufacture of biologicals, biotechnological products
and their intermediates.
(v) To evolve safety guidelines for biotechnology Research and Development and manufacturing
in India.
(vi) To act as the central agency for the import of genetically manipulated materials, culture, cells,
specimens, tissues and biotech products including DNA and RNA of any type or size and for
promoting their production in the country.
(vii) To serve as the inter-ministerial and inter-agency nodal point for all specific international
bilateral and multilateral Research and Development collaborations and agreements in the area
of biotechnology; act as the nodal point for all technology transfers in the area of biotechnology.
(viii) To manufacture and ensure application of recombinant, cell-based and DNA vaccines, diagnostics
and other biotechnological products.
(ix) To evolve programmes for Human Resource Development in the area of biotechnology.
(x) To serve as an administrative and implementing Department of agencies, commissions, boards,
etc. specifically formed by the Government for fulfilling the national objectives in biotechnology
and also to serve as the nodal point for Bio-informatics including training and creation of
infrastructure, collection, dissemination and exchange of information relating to biotechnology.
(xi) Establishment of National Biotechnology Regulatory Authority
(xii) Matters relating to:
• International Centre for Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology (ICGEB), New Delhi;

2
• National Institute of Immunology (NII), New Delhi;
• National Centre for Cell Sciences (NCCS), Pune;
• Centre for DNA Fingerprinting and Diagnostics (CDFD), Hyderabad;
• National Institute for Plant Genome Research (NIPGR), New Delhi;
• National Brain Research Centre (NBRC), Manesar, Gurgaon;
• Institute for Bioresource and Sustainable Development (IBSD), Imphal
• Institute of Life Sciences (ILS), Bhubaneswar
• Translational Research in Health Science and Technology Institute, Faridabad
• Rajiv Gandhi Centre for Biotechnology, Trivananthpuram
• UNESCO Regional Centre for Education, Training and Innovation in Biotechnology,
Faridabad
• National Institute of Biomedical Genomics, Kolkata
• Institute for Stem Cell Science and Regenerative Medicine, Bangalore
• National Agri-Food Biotechnology Institute Mohali, Punjab

1.1 The vision of the Department is to create biotechnology tools and technologies that address the
problems of agriculture productivity, food production, nutrition security, health care and environmental
sustainability by providing new and emerging products and services at affordable prices, generate
employment opportunities and make India globally competitive in the emerging bio-economy.

has been successfully achieving its targeted goals and objectives for biotechnology based development
of NER including Sikkim. Some achievements are: more than 600 NER scientists/researchers/faculty,
creation of best of the R&D infrastructure at almost all R&D institutions and universities of NER through
equipment support, setting up of Centre of Excellence (CoEs) as well as setting up of Units of Excellence
(U-Excel) around meritorious scientists, training of NER scientists/faculty in reputed overseas institutions
and specialised training of scientists/ researchers/students under various schemes/programmes. 88 Senior
Secondary Schools from NER have been selected for setting up of Biotechnology Labs under
"Biotechnology Labs in Senior Secondary Schools (BLiSS)" Programme. During 2015-16, 15 Scientists/
Faculty have been selected for bringing advancement in the Biotechnology and Life Science related
activities in various institutions of research and higher learning in the NER under "DBT-NER Visiting
Research Professorship (VRP) Programme".
11.2 The major programmes implemented during 2015-16 are Flagship TWINNING R&D programme
to facilite collaborative studies between labs in NER and institutions from the rest of India with more
than 350 such network projects; a collaborative research programme on Chemical Ecology of North
Eastern Region has been initiated in collaboration with leading institutions (IISc, NCBS, UAS) and NER

15
institutions; 14 scientists/faculty have been selected for "Visiting Research Professorship (VRP)"; 41
Scientists of NER were awarded Overseas Associateship through a special programme of DBT's
Biotechnology Overseas Associateship; a DBT partnership Center of Excellence on Fisheries & Aquaculture
Biotechnology (COE-FAB) has been established at College of Fisheries, CAU, Lembucherra; a regional
level Animal House Facility is funded in Dibrugarh; a DBT-NER Centre for Advanced Animal Diagnostics
and Services on Animal Health and Diseases (ADSAHD) is being established in NER involving all eight
States and few specialised laboratories from other parts of the country; a modern Regional X-Ray
Crystallography Facility has been established at IIT Guwahati as a regional facility and being used by
the NER researchers; and over 150 training programmes have been conducted for NER scientists/
researchers/students by biotech hub network in NER. The Department of Biotechnology further stated
that during this short span of time, the NER researchers have been able to publish more than 400
research papers in the peer reviewed journals besides presentation of papers in the national as well as
international conferences.
11.3 The Committee feels that 10% allocation of the total budget towards biotechnology backed
development activities in the North Eastern region of the country is certainly a boon for the
development of scientific activities in the region. The Committee recommends that the Department
should intensify its efforts and ensure that the requisite 10% allocation of budget is fully utilised
towards the proposed activities. Further, the Department should in coordination with other
scientific Departments, make efforts for creation of skilled human resource and setting up of
institutional resources for much needed growth in this region.
PUBLICITY TO THE SCHEMES AND PUBLIC AWARENESS
12. During the meeting of the Committee held on the 30th March, 2016, the Committee expressed
concern that inspite of initiating a lot of schemes/programmes for the benefit of the underprivileged
people and the society, the Department was not able to effectively communicate its achievements and
schemes/programmes etc. to the people at large. Even the Members of the Standing Committee/other
MPs as well as State Government officials were ignorant and unaware of the schemes initiated by the
Union Department of Biotechnology. One of the Members of the Committee cited an incident wherein
during a district level meeting with various departments of State Government, he found that the District
Collector and other district level officers present in the meeting were unaware of the schemes of the
Central Government launched for the benefit of the society at large.
12.1 The Committee is aware that the Department undertakes many programmes which aim to
create a platform for self-employment generation among the target population and diffusion of
proven and field tested technologies through demonstration, training and extension activities.
The Committee is of the opinion that there is a need to give publicity to the research activities
undertaken by the Department and the schemes/programmes of the Department for the benefit
of the people. State Governments, especially North-Eastern States, should be informed of these
schemes so that the benefit of the schemes could reach those for whom these are intended. The
Committee is of the view that the information regarding the schemes/programmes of the
Department must reach down to the lowest level even if it is not beneficial straightaway. The
Committee recommends that there should be a specific provision for publicity to the schemes/

16
programmes of the Department in the budget allocation of every Ministry/Department so that
the activities of the Department could reach the common people and that the required funds for
the purpose should be made available to the Department. In order to filter down the information
to the grassroots level, the Department should also have regular meetings with the members of
the standing Committee and other MPs to brief them about these schemes so that they could
communicate the same to the people in their constituency for their effective utilisation.
NATIONAL BIOTECHNOLOGY DEVELOPMENT STRATEGY 2015-20
13. The Committee desired to know the aims and objectives of the National Biotechnology Development
Strategy 2015-20 and the long and short term plans envisaged by the Department to achieve the said
objectives. The Committee was informed that the envisaged mission of the National Biotechnology
Development Strategy (NBDS) 2015-20 are providing impetus to utilising the knowledge and tools to the
advantage of Humanity; Launch a major well directed mission backed with significant investment for
generation of new Biotech Products; Empower scientifically and technologically India's incomparable
Human Resource; Create a strong Infrastructure for R&D and Commercialisation; and establish India as
a world class Bio-manufacturing Hub.
13.1 The key elements of the Strategy are: Building a Skilled Workforce and Leadership; Revitalizing the
knowledge environment at par with the growing bio economy; Enhance Research opportunities in basic,
disciplinary and inter-disciplinary sciences; Encourage use-inspired discovery research; Focus on
biotechnology tools for inclusive development; Nurturing innovation, translational capacity and
entrepreneurship; Ensuring a transparent, efficient and Regulatory system of global standard and
communication strategy; Biotechnology cooperation - Fostering global and national alliances; Strengthen
Institutional Capacity with redesigned governance models; and Create a matrix of measurement of
processes as well as outcome.
13.2 The Committee desired to know the budgetary provisions made by the Department in 2016-17 to
pursue the objectives of the strategy. The Department informed that the new strategy will have financial
implications from the financial year 2016-17 which is also the last year of 12th Plan (2012-17). To initiate
the programmes of the strategy, initial seed money has been provided in relevant schemes particularly
Biotechnology Research and Development; and Biotech Industrial Development and Entrepreneurship. It
was also informed that the strategy would require major allocations for the period 2017-2020.
13.3 The Committee is of the view that biotechnology is the technology of the future and hopes
that National Biotechnology Development Strategy 2015-20 would play a key role in establishing
India as a world class Biotechnology hub. The Committee recommends that the Government
should provide adequate financial allocations for the implementation of the strategy in the years
to come.
GENERAL OBSERV ATION
14. The Department of Biotechnology, Ministry of Science and Technology plays a pivotal role
in the promotion of biotechnology in the country. New initiatives in the field of biotechnology

17
play a significant role in the development of a nation, be it in the field of agriculture, education,
medicine, economy, sports, games, jobs or tourism, etc. All the great scientific discoveries and
technological achievements in our country have improved the Indian economic status and have
created many new ways for the new generations to grow in the technologically advanced
environment. The Committee is of the view that although the Department has undertaken
accelerated efforts for achieving excellence in the field of biotechnology, a lot more needs to be
done and achieved in this sector. In order to successfully meet the challenges of the future, the
Committee recommends that the Department should undertake meaningful initiatives to establish
strong foundations for a leadership role in the world in various areas of biotechnology.

FINANCIAL PERFORMANCE OF THE DEPARTMENT
The Committee feels that the purpose of Five Year Plans is to formulate long gestation
projects and the inadequate allocation of funds during the plan period adversely affects the
execution of projects. The Committee is disappointed to note that instead of being provided the
approved allocation, the Department of Biotechnology has been allocated only 62.70 percent of
its approved outlay during the 12th Five Year Plan. This would certainly have an adverse bearing
on the schemes/programmes of the Department in the 12th Five Year Plan. (Para 2.2)
The Committee notes that the actual expenditure of the Department has gone down from
99.19 percent in 2013-14 to 96.36 percent and 92.13 percent in 2014-15 and 2015-16 respectively.
The Department's performance of utilising 99.19 percent of its allocation in 2013-14 indicates
that it has the capability of fully utilising the resources made available to it. However, the
Department failed to rise to its true potential and could expend only 92.13% of the allocated
resources till 28.3.2016. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should
review its financial performance during 2015-16 and try to identify the bottlenecks responsible
for not optimally utilising the funds made available to it, so as to avoid its recurrence in future.
(Para 2.3)
BUDGET ALLOCATION FOR THE YEAR 2016-17
The Committee notes that unlike previous years of the 12th Five Year Plan, the allocation
of the Department was not reduced at RE stage during 2015-16. The Department has indicated
the requirement of an additional amount of ````` 200 crore to implement mission programmes in
live-stock and pulses and other inter-ministerial programmes. Keeping in view the fact that a
large amount of its allocation promised for the 12th Five Year Plan is yet to be disbursed to the
Department, the Committee recommends that the plan allocation of the Department should be
suitably augmented at RE stage to enable the Department to achieve its desired objectives.
(Para 3.3)
MONITORING MECHANISM OF THE DEPARTMENT
The existence of a strong and effective monitoring mechanism to monitor and review the
progress of ongoing schemes and programmes is extremely important. The Committee recommends
that the Department of Biotechnology should periodically monitor all its schemes and programmes
and take corrective measures, wherever required, so as to ensure that all its schemes/programmes
proceed as per the schedule. (Para 4.1)
HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (HRD)
The Committee has noted the performance of the Department on Human Resource
Development during the last three years. Since human resources form the backbone of research
activities, the Committee recommends that the Department should continue to optimally utilise
the allocation made for HRD internally by it. The Committee notes the schemes/programmes of
the Department to encourage, nurture and involve talented researches in scientific pursuits. The

training courses, fellowships and awards providing industrial training to students etc. is
commendable. The Committee is of the view that biotechnology will play a major role in scientific
activities in the years to come and recommends that keeping in view the increased requirement
of human resources in the Biotechnology sector in the future, the Department should undertake
a review of its existing capacity to generate human resources and expand its extant infrastructure
to cater to the additional requirement of personnel and provide the requisite quality human
resource in biotechnology sector. The Committee also feels that more allocation is required for
the purpose. (Para 5.7)

The Committee feels that the reasons furnished by the Department for underutilisation of
funds under 'Biotechnology for Societal Development' are not convincing. Further, in view of the
underutilisation by the Department under this programme during 2013-14 and 2014-15, the
Committee is not inclined to accept the view expressed by the Department that balance amount
under the head will be fully utilised. The aim of the programme is to promote use of biotechnological
processes and tools for the benefit of the disadvantaged sections of the society comprising of
women, rural population and SCs/STs and any underutilisation of the funds allocated for the
programme directly affects these underprivileged sections of the country. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Department should undertake a periodic review of the progress of the
programmes under the head and ensure that there is no underutilisation of the funds allocated

that there has been gross underutilisation of funds in this programme and the contention of the
Department that there was no adverse effect on the overall goals and scope of bioclusters, is not

a mechanism to maintain data on patents filed/granted even though it supports various projects
of different universities, institutes and non-profit scientific organisations. The Committee is of

advancement of a country. In the absence of any reliable data, it is not possible to undertake
a conclusive analysis of the scientific achievements of the Department in this field. The Committee,

keep a record of the patents filed and granted, both in India and abroad, by the institutions

The Committee observes that the number of patents filed (national) dropped from 70 in
2013-14 to 33 in 2015-16. Similarly, the number of patents filed (foreign) dipped from 18 in

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairperson of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and
Technology, Environment and Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on
its behalf, present this Two Hundred Seventy-ninth Report of the Committee. This Report deals with the

REPORT
INTRODUCTION
The remarkable achievements of Indian Space Programme since independence of India have
demonstrated India’s technological capability and strength in the world. These Space Programmes are
implemented and executed by the Department of Space since its establishment in June, 1972. The programmes
framed by the Space Commission are carried out through the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)
and the Grant-in-aid institutions, i.e., Physical Research Laboratory (PRL), National Atmospheric Research
Laboratory (NARL), North Eastern Space Applications Centre (NE-SAC), Semi Conductor Laboratory (SCL)
and Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology (IIST) with Department of Space Secretariat and the
Headquarters of ISRO in Bengaluru, Karnataka.
1.1 The Programme offices at ISRO Headquarters co-ordinate the overall programmes including
Satellite Communication, Satellite Navigation, Earth Observation, Launch Vehicle, Space Science,
Atmospheric Science, Space Industry Development, Disaster Management Support, International Co-
Operation, Publications And Public Relations, Budget and Economic Analysis and Human Resource
Development.
1.2 The successful completion of intended six month period by Mars Orbiter Spacecraft in its orbit
around Planet Mars, making India the first country to achieve total success in its maiden attempt to explore
the planet of Mars, is one of the most remarkable achievements of the Department of Space. Besides, launch
of GSLV -MK II carrying the indigenous Cryogenic Upper Stage (CUS), ASTROSAT-India’s first Multi
wavelength Space Observatory, IRNSS -ID, IRNSS -1E and IRNSS -1F and GSAT -15 carrying
communication satellite and GAGAN payload and other missions and programmes are the highlights of the
achievements of Department of Space in the financial year 2015-16.
OBJECTIVES OF INDIAN SPACE PROGRAMME
2. The primary objective of the Indian Space Programme is to promote the development and
application of space technology and space science for the socio-economic benefits of the nation through
establishment of operational space services in a self-reliant manner. The main thrust areas of the programme
are:
 Satellite-based communication and navigation for various applications.
 Satellite-based resources survey and management and environmental monitoring.
 Meteorological applications.
 Space Science Research and Planetary Exploration; and
 Development and operationalisation of indigenously built satellites, launch vehicles and associated
ground segment for providing these space-based services.
2.1 The major centres, units and establishments of DoS/ISRO, responsible for carrying out R&D activities
as well as for undertaking various projects and programmes, are as under:-
(i) Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (VSSC), Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala provides the technology
base for the country’s indigenous launch vehicle (rocket) development;

2
(ii) Liq uid Propulsion Systems Centre (LPSC), with its facilities at Bengaluru, and Valiamala/
Thiruvananthapuram is responsible for development of liquid propulsion and cryogenic
propulsion systems for satellite launch vehicles;
(iii) ISRO Propulsion Complex (IPRC), erstwhile LPSC, Mahendragiri has the responsibility for
assembly, integration and testing of storable and cryogenic liquid rocket engines and stages,
space craft thrusters testing in sea level and high altitude conditions, storage of liquid and
cryogenic propellants and production of liquid hydrogen etc.
(iv) Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC-SHAR) at Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh, is the launch
base and also provides the facilities for processing of solid rocket motors;
(v) ISRO Satellite Centre (ISAC), Bengaluru is entrusted with the prime responsibility of the satellite
development;
(vi) Laboratory for Electro-Optic Systems (LEOS), Bengaluru, is responsible for development and
production of electro-optical sensors for satellites;
(vii) Space Applications Centre (SAC), Ahmedabad, Gujarat carries out R&D in space applications
as well as development of application payloads;
(viii) Development and Educational Communication Unit (DECU), Ahmedabad is involved in the
conception, definition, planning and socio/techno-economic evaluation of developmental space
applications;
(ix) National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC), Hyderabad, Andhra Pradesh is responsible for satellite
data acquisition and processing, data dissemination, aerial remote sensing and decision support
for disaster management;
(x) Indian Institute of Remote Sensing (IIRS), Dehradun, Uttrakhand is a premier training and
educational institute set up for honing skills of trained professionals in the field of Remote
Sensing, Geoinformatics and Global Positioning System (GPS) Technology for Natural
Resources, Environmental and Disaster Management;
(xi) ISRO Telemetry, Tracking and Command Network (ISTRAC), with its ground stations at
Bengaluru, Sriharikota, Lucknow, Bearslake (USA), Biak (Indonesia), Brunei, Mauritius, Port
Blair and Thiruvananthapuram provides the telemetry, track and command support and
spacecraft mission management for Indian remote sensing satellite missions, space science
missions and satellite launch vehicle programmes;
(xii) Master Control Facility (MCF) with its main facility at Hassan, Karnataka and backup facility
at Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh have the responsibility for control and operation of INSAT/GSAT/
METSAT satellites; and
(xiii) ISRO Inertial Systems Unit (IISU), Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala carries out research and
development in the area of inertial systems for satellites and launch vehicles.
2.2 A National Natural Resources Management Systems (NNRMS), with DoS as the nodal agency,
has been established to ensure optimal management/utilisation of natural resources using remote

3
sensing data in conjunction with conventional techniques. Under NNRMS, five Regional Remote
Sensing Service Centres (RRSSCs) at Bengaluru, Dehradun, Jodhpur, Kharagpur and Nagpur have
also been set up for the execution of remote sensing application programmes in the respective regions.
With effect from December 2009, four out of five RRSSCs have been redesignated as Regional
Remote Sensing Centres (RRSCs), while RRSSC, Dehradun has been merged with Indian Institute
of Remote Sensing (IIRS).
2.3 The mandate of the organisations receiving Grants-in-aid from Department of Space is as
follows:
(i) Physical Research Laboratory (PRL), Ahmedabad, an autonomous institution supported mainly
by the Department of Space, carries out research in space sciences;
(ii) The National Atmospheric Research Laboratory (NARL), set up at Gadanki near Tirupati,
conducts atomospheric research;
(iii) The North-Eastern Space Applications Centre (NE-SAC), established as an autonomous body
under the Department of Space, provides space technology inputs for developmental activities
in the North-Eastern Region;
(iv) The Semi-conductor Laboratory, Chandigarh, an R&D society, is entrusted with the
design and development of V ery Large Scale Integrated Circuit (VLSI) devices and
development of micro-electronic systems to meet the strategic needs of the country;
and
(v) The Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology (IIST), an autonomous body under the
Department, aims at creating quality human resources tuned to suit the requirements of state-
of-the-art space research programme. The Institute offers graduate, post-graduate and doctoral
programmes in the area of space science, technology and applications. Initially, IIST started
the courses from the academic year 2007-08 with the existing infrastructure at
Thiruvananthapuram.
2.4 The ANTRIX Corporation Limited, Bengaluru, established in September, 1992, a wholly owned
Government of India company under the administrative control of Department of Space, is a marketing arm
of ISRO for promotion and commercial exploitation of Space products, technical consultancy services and
transfer of technologies developed by ISRO. It also facilitates development of Space related capabilities in
India.
2.5 Besides, the RESPOND programme of ISRO supports sponsored research activities in space science,
space applications and space technology in several national academic/research institutions and Space
Technology Cells in premier technological institutes of the country through grants-in-aid.

GEOSTATIONARY SATELLITE LAUNCH VEHICLE (GSLV)
10. Geosynchronous Satellite launch V ehicle (GSLV) is a three-stage vehicle with solid, liquid and cryogenic
upper stage, designed to place 2 ton class of communication satellite in the Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit
(GTO).
10.1 The fi rst flight of GSLV took place from SDSC-SHAR on April 18, 2001 by launching 1540 kg
GSA T-1. Eight more launches have taken place, GSLV D2 on May 8, 2003 (GSAT – 2 1825 kg), GSLV-F01
on September 20, 2004 (EDUSAT 1950 kg), GSLV – F02 on July 10, 2006, GSLV – F04 on September 2,
2007 (INSAT – 4CR 2130 kg), GSLV – D3 on April 15, 2010, GSLV – F06 on December 25, 2010, GSLV
– D5 on 5January, 2014 and GSLV-D6 on 27August, 2015.
10.2 It was informed by the Department that GSLV -D6 with indigenous Cryogenic Upper Stage (CUS),
successfully launched GSAT-6, an advanced communication satellite of 2117 kg into GTO and the launch
signified a major step in perfecting highly complex cryogenic propulsion technology and also achieving self-
reliance in launching 2 ton class communication satellites into GTO.
10.3 GSLV-MK III is the next generation launch vehicle of ISRO capable of launching 4 ton class of
satellite to Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit (GTO). It is a three stage vehicle with two solid motor strap-ons
(S200), a liquid propellant core stage (L110) and a cryogenic stage (C25). The solid motors and liquid
propellant core stages were successfully flight tested in the sub-orbital GSLV -MK III X mission during
December, 2014.
10.4 The Committee desired to know the progress made in the development of Cryogenic Stage (C 25).
The Department informed that it has undergone a series of ignition tests in 2015, including a flight
duration test for 635 sec. and an endurance test for a duration of 800 sec and on February 19, 2016, the
second cryogenic engine was successfully tested for the full flight duration of 635 sec. The activities
related to the integration of the engine with the Cryogenic Stage are in progress and the Cryogenic Stage
is expected to be hot tested in the second half of 2016, before it is inducted into the GSLV MkIII launch
vehicle.
10.5 The Committee feels that GSLV-MK III is a successful accomplishment of the Department
exhibiting India’s might in the world in launching next generation launch vehicle with indigenously
developed cryogenic engine. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the testing of cryogenic
engine and its induction into the GSLV-MK III launch vehicle should be speeded up and completed
by the Department within its scheduled time frame.

TRISONIC WIND TUNNEL PROJECT
11. Trisonic Wind Tunnel facility is planned to be set up at Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre,
Thiruvananthapuram for meeting the test requirements of future launch vehicle development.
11.1 The Committee desired to know the details of the project’s application and its significance. The
Department informed that the project is for wind tunnel testing which is an integral part of the design and
development process in aerospace industry and the data generated by testing provide aerodynamic
characterisation which form major inputs for the structural design of satellite launch vehicles.
11.2 The Department further informed the Committee that even in an age of advanced computer simulation,
aerospace engineers still rely on the testing of physical models to verify the computer data and establish
baseline aerodynamic information. Space vision for the future emphasizes the enhancement of launch vehicle
capability, reusable launch vehicle and human rated launch vehicle. Demand on wind tunnel testing and
computations for aero characterisation for re-entry and human rated vehicle are of higher magnitude than
the expendable launch vehicle. Generation of more reliable, high quality experimental aerodynamic data
through testing in more than one wind tunnel facility mainly for complex missions involving humans is
essential to improve safety and reliability.
11.3 The Committee was informed by the Department that during the processing, a revision in scope was
envisaged to include the facility for the simulation of jet-on effects and therefore the revised project report
has been submitted for financial sanction and is under process.
11.4 The Committee had, in its 255
th Report on Demands for Grants (2015-16) of Department of
Space, considered the subject and highlighted that budget provision for the project in 2014-15 could
not be utilised due to the inability of the Department to obtain necessary approvals. The Committee
had therefore recommended that the approval for the project should be obtained at the earliest.

SATELLITE NA VIGATION PROGRAMME
14. Satellite Navigation (SATNAV) is a programme that includes activities such as GAGAN and Indian
Regional Navigation Satellite System (IRNSS). GAGAN is the first satellite-based augmentation navigation
system over Indian region and it aims to provide Satellite -based Navigation services with accuracy and
integrity required for civil aviation applications and to provide better Air Traffic management over Indian
Airspace. Establishment of an independent Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System (IRNSS) is going to
provide accurate position information service to users in India as well as the region extending up to 1500 km
from its boundary, which is its primary service area.
14.1 The Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System (IRNSS) is planned to be a constellation of 7
satellites aimed at providing position accuracies similar to Global Positioning System (GPS) in a region
centred around India with a coverage extending upto 1500 km from India. IRNSS will provide two types
of services namely, Standard Positioning Service (SPS) for common civilian users and Restricted Service
(RS) for special authorised users and is expected to provide a position accuracy of better than 20 m in the
primary service area. The IRNSS system mainly consists of Ground Segment, Space Segment and User
Segment.
14.2 Segment of IRNSS consists of seven satellites with three to be put in geostationary orbit and four in
inclined Geosynchronous orbit. IRNSS – 1A, the first of the seven satellites of the IRNSS Constellation,
was successfully launched onboard PSLV-C22 on July 01, 2013 and is functioning satisfactorily. IRNSS-1B
and IRNSS-1C were also launched successfully in 2014. IRNSS – 1B was launched by PSLV-C24 on April
4, 2014 and IRNSS-1C on board PSLV-C26 on October 16, 2014.  The satellites, IRNSS-1D was successfully
launched on 29
th March 2015 and IRNSS -1E on 20 th January, 2016. Also, IRNSS -1F was launched on
March 10, 2016.
14.3 The Committee desired to know the status of launch of IRNSS -1F and IRNSS -1G and about the
realization of IRNSS constellation by the end of 2016. In response, the Department informed the Committee
that IRNSS -1G is planned to be launched during April, 2016 and with these launches, the IRNSS constellation
is planned to be completed by April 2016.
14.4 The Committee desired to know the progress made with regard to the ground control centres specially
the primary control station at MCF and backup control centre in Bhopal. The Department informed that all
primary facilities for managing IRNSS constellation and the required ground stations and control centres at
MCF, Hassan and Bhopal are ready and the new Spacecraft Control Centre at MCF, Hassan is planned to be
ready by end March, 2016. The Department also informed the Committee that the additional ISRO Navigation
Centre (INC) and IRNSS Network Timing Centre at Lucknow are planned to be ready by September 2016
and April 2017, respectively.
14.5 The Committee congratulates the Department on the successful launch of IRNSS-1G . The
Committee is of the view that with this launch, India will have an independent robust navigation
system which is a significant achievment for the country. The Committee, however, recommends
that the Department should make efforts to complete the additional ISRO Navigation Centre (INC)
and IRNSS Network Timing Centre at Lucknow in scheduled time frame which will assist in
functioning and operation of navigation system.

RECOMMENDA TION/OBSERV ATIONS — A T A GLANCE
FINANCIAL PERFORMANCE OF THE DEPARTMENT
The Committee takes note of the fact that the cuts in the budgetary grants at the R.E. stage
in financial years 2013-14 and 2015-16 were above `````1600 crore and `````1400 crores respectively which
results into delays and disruption in launching of crucial programmes of strategic importance.
However, in 2015-16, the allocation was reduced by ````` 428.75 crore. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the cuts in the grants at R.E. stage should be avoided so that the Department
could continue with work as per the priorities set by it without any obstacles of resource crunch. In
addition the Department should also be provided adequate funds to undertake all its critical
programmes and schemes in right earnest. (Para 4.1)
BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2016-17
The Committee strongly recommends that the Government should positively consider the
requirement of additional funds for the Department in order to facilitate undertaking works of
strategic importance. (Para 5.2)
PHYSICAL ACHIEVEMENTS OF THE DEPARTMENT IN 2015-16
The Committee takes note of the achievements of the Department in 2015-16. Launching
of ASTROSAT, India’s first space observatory, near completion of Indian Regional navigation
Satellite System and launching of some of the important communication satellites has
demonstrated India’s potential to become a world leader in Space Technology. The Committee
strongly feels that such achievements should not only be continued but should also be sustained
and improved so as to make India self-reliant, self independent and successful in its space
missions. (Para 6.1)
POLAR SATELLITE LAUNCH VEHICLES
The Committee strongly recommends that a crucial programme of PSLV launches should not
be subjected to resource crunch. Considered as a work horse, PSLV have been extremely successful
in launching most of the significant satellites of India and hence, the Committee recommends that
the programme should not face reduction in budgetary allocation at R.E. stage which would cause
disruption and delays in launches. (Para 9.5)
GEOSTATIONARY SATELLITE LAUNCH VEHICLE (GSLV)
The Committee feels that GSLV-MK III is a successful accomplishment of the Department
exhibiting India’s might in the world in launching next generation launch vehicle with indigenously
developed cryogenic engine. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the testing of cryogenic
engine and its induction into the GSLV-MK III launch vehicle should be speeded up and completed
by the Department within its scheduled time frame. (Para 10.5)
The Committee feels that the adequate budgetary allocation to an important programme
like GSLV-MKIII Development should always be made available to the Department to ensure
expeditious completion of the programme. Since a reduced allocation has been made for the
programme in 2016-17, the Committee recommends that no cuts in budgetary grants in the
21

22
programme should be made at the R.E. stage in 2016-17 so that the progress of the programme is
not adversely affected. (Para 10.8)
TRISONIC  WIND TUNNEL PROJECT
The Committee had, in its 255 th Report on Demands for Grants (2015-16) of Department of
Space, considered the subject and highlighted that budget provision for the project in 2014-15 could
not be utilised due to the inability of the Department to obtain necessary approvals. The Committee
had therefore recommended that the approval for the project should be obtained at the earliest. The
Committee is, however, constrained to note that despite the recommendation, the financial approval
is still awaited which is delaying the programme. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
Department should exhibit its zeal and obtain all the approvals at the earliest so that the programme
takes off without further delay. (Para 11.4)
MANNED  MISSION/HUMAN SPACE FLIGHT PROGRAMME
The Committee notes that the pre-project activities are still in progress and critical technologies
like Crew Escape System (CES) and Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS) are

Manned Mission/Human Space Flight Programme will not be accomplished. (Para 12.4)
The Committee takes note of the Department’s inability to utilize the funds and its failure to
make best use of the funds available to it for completion of the project in 2015-16, as a result of
which the funds were reduced at R.E. stage. The Committee recommends that the Department
should take the programme seriously and should make full utilization of the funds made available
to it. (Para 12.5)
RADAR IMAGING SATELLITE – RISAT – 1A
The Committee is of the view that RISAT-1A is an important satellite having applications in
agriculture, forests and in disaster management and therefore its launch is significant for its
contribution in the said fields. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Department should
take required steps for the completion of the programme within its scheduled time frame.
(Para 13.3)
The Committee notes that inspite of having augmented the budget allocation for the project
at R.E. 2015-16 to ````` 10.20 crore to meet the requirements towards initial milestone payments for
procurement for long lead electronic equipments, the Department has not been able to utilise any
amount till February, 2016.  The Committee recommends that the Department should make sure
that all necessary efforts are made to achieve the desired targets of the project in 2016-17 and there
is no underutilisation of funds. (Para 13.4)
SATELLITE NAVIGATION PROGRAMME
The Committee congratulates the Department on the successful launch of IRNSS-1G . The
Committee is of the view that with this launch, India will have an independent robust navigation
system which is a significant achievment for the country. The Committee, however, recommends

23
that the Department should make efforts to complete the additional ISRO Navigation Centre (INC)
and IRNSS Network Timing Centre at Lucknow in scheduled time frame which will assist in
functioning and operation of navigation system. (Para 14.5)
SPACE SCIENCES - ASTROSAT MISSION
The Committee notes that the budget allocations for the Astrosat Mission, which was reduced
during 2014-15 and 2015-16, at R.E. stage could not be fully utilized by the Department. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should go all-out to avoid underutilisation
of the allocated funds. (Para 15.2)
INDIAN LUNAR MISSION – CHANDRAYAAN-2
The Committee notes the increased allocation to the programme in 2016-17 and recommends
that the Department should utilise the allocated budget in an optimal manner so that the Orbiter,
Lander and Rover modules of the mission are realized without any delay. (Para 16.3)
The Committee is of the opinion that completing the mission Chandrayaan-2 indigenously is
both a challenge and an opportunity before the Department and with its completion, India’s capability
in launch technology will be proved. However, the Committee notes that the mission is far behind
the targeted schedule and therefore, recommends that the Department should take steps to speed
up the stages of development of the project and complete the designs and testing of the components
to ensure its targeted launch by first half of 2018. (Para 16.6)
NASA ISRO SYNTHETIC APERTURE RADAR MISSION (NISAR)
The Committee notes that the allocation for NISAR was reduced to nearly half at R.E. stage,
out of which only a meagre amount of ````` 1.91 crore could be utilised by the Department upto February
2016. The reasons furnished by the Department indicated that either the Department could not
realistically plan the various stages of the programme or could not meet the schedule of events of
the project. The Committee recommends that the Department should monitor the progress of the
programme through an institutional mechanism and ensure that the funds allocated for the project
during 2016-17 are utilised optimally. (Para 17.5)
SATELLITE FOR SAARC  COUNTRIES
The Committee notes the progress achieved in obtaining concurrence and signing of crucial
agreements with some SAARC countries i.e. Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, and Nepal. The Committee,
however, notes that agreement with other countries, alongwith Afghanistan, are still being pursued
and recommends that the other countries should be actively pursued so that concurrence from all
SAARC members is obtained at the earliest and the funds earmarked for the project are realised.
(Para 18.4)
SPACE APPLICATIONS - CONTRIBUTION TO THE SOCIETY
The Committee notes the application of the spin-off technologies in the sectors of agriculture
and irrigation, which are the backbone of India’s economy, and feels that the Department has the
potential to enhance the space applications in these sectors which would tremendously contribute to
growth of the economy of the country at large. The Committee recommends that the Department
should make more efforts in enlarging space applications and in pursuing projects which involve
societal and economical benefits. (Para 19.7)

24
The Committee had recommended in its 255 th Report that the Department of Space should
avoid reduction in Development & Educational Unit (DECU) and other programmes of societal
benefit. The Committee, however, observes substantial reduction in budgetary allocations to
Development & Educational Unit (DECU) programme and also notes underutilization in many
projects of Space applications. The Committee recommends that the policy framework for SATCOM
based societal applications should be finalised at the earliest. The Committee also recommends that
the Department should take all measures to avoid underutilization of funds available at the
Department’s disposal which adversely affects the programmes having long term societal benefits.
(Para 19.11)
DISASTER MANAGEMENT SUPPORT
The Committee notes the work done by the Department in the monitoring of Chennai floods
of 2015 and also steps taken to improve Flood Warning Systems. The Committee is of the view that
floods can cause damage to lives and property and recommends that the Department should provide
all necessary support and strengthen early flood warning systems and detection of unseasonal floods
and rainfall to minimise the loss in case of such natural calamities. (Para 19.16)
SPACE PROGRAMME AND INDUSTRY PARTICIPATION
The Committee notes that the recommendations of the Internal Committee on supporting
Start-Ups in Space Sector is still under review. The Committee feels that encouraging start-ups by
the Department would foster indigenous capability in space related manufacturing sector. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the recommendations of the Internal Committee should
be reviewed at the earliest and efforts should be made to give a boost to the start-ups.
(Para 20.2)
NATIONAL SPACE ACT OF INDIA
The Committee feels that a National Space Act of India would be beneficial for the overall
growth of Space activities facilitating participation of both public and private sectors, enforcing
commercialization including better delivery of space services and supervision and regulation of
space related activities. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should take
all necessary action for the enactment of the law at the earliest. (Para 21.3)

INTRODUCTION

I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Science and Technology, Environment and Forests having been authorised by the
Committee to present the report on its behalf, present the Twenty-eighth Report of the
Committee. This Report deals with the issues contained in the Annual Report (1993-94) of
the Department of Electronics with reference to: (i) Software Technology Parks (STP); (ii)
Electronic Hardware Technology Parks (EHTPs); (iii) Electronics for Weaker Sections
including Women; (iv) Employment Potential of Electronics; and (v) Support of the
Department of Electronics for R&D, particularly with regard to the Technology
Development Council (TDC), National Radar Council (NRC) and Industrial Promotion.

2. The Committee held in all three meetings on January 5, 6 and June 19, 1995. In the
meeting held on January 5, 1995 the Secretary, Department of Electronics made a brief
presentation about the activities of his Department, particularly with reference to the
aforementioned five areas and the Members raised certain points thereon. On January 6,
1995 further discussion was held and the Committee heard the replies of the Secretary and
other officials of the Department of Electronics to the points raised by the Members.

3. The Committee thanks the Officials of the Department of Electronics for giving it
necessary information and placing before it relevant papers/background notes which
facilitated detailed examination of the Annual Report (1993-94) of the Department.

4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on the 19th
June, 1995.
