18. LASER INTERFEROMETER GRA VITATIONAL-WA VE OBSERVATORY (LIGO) FACILITY
18.1 The Committee was informed that a new advanced Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave
Observatory (LIGO) is being set up in India. This is the third such detector in the world, the other

34
two being in the United States. It was informed by the Department that Americans are providing
India the detector for LIGO facility. Nine Institutions of the Department of Atomic energy are
actively working on the LIGO Project.
18.2 According to the Department, 37 Indian scientists have contributed towards the recent discovery
of gravitational waves. Steps have been taken by the gravitational wave community of the country
for forging international scientific collaborations and developing human resource in this field. For
this, a pan-Indian consortium, Indian Initiative in Gravitational-wave Observations (IndIGO) was
formed consisting of researchers from premier institutions and universities of the country in 2009.
IndIGO consortium has representation in the Gravitational Waves International Committee (GWIC)
which works to facilitate international collaboration and cooperation in the construction, operation
and use of the major gravitational wave detection facilities world-wide. Indian scientists are participating
in the international LIGO Science Collaboration (LSC), through IndIGO.
18.3 As regards benefit to India, it has been informed by the Department that LIGO-India will be
an important project in the field of fundamental sciences in the country. During the meeting held
on 13
th February, 2017 informing about the LIGO facility, the Secretary, Department of Atomic
Energy said the following information:-
“Sir, the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) facility, as I had
pointed out, would be the third in the world. There are already two in America, where, for
the first time, they detected the gravitational wave. This would be the third country. And the
advantage of this third centre would be that whatever number they detect —for two three
years, they have been detecting one wave —this number would increase to one or two per
month or one or two per 15 days. So, there would be a large number of increase in the
number of gravitational waves detected. That is what the interest of the Americans is in
giving us the detector.”
18.4 The Committee is happy to note that India has been selected as the host country of
only third LIGO facility in the world. Indian scientists must take up this opportunity and
utilise the goodwill and advantage. The Committee hopes that India will take advantage of
LIGO facility and become a force to reckon with in study of gravitational waves.

20.1 T ata Memorial Centre is an autonomous body under the Department of Atomic Energy. It

F. UTILISATION OF NON-POWER APPLICATIONS (NPAs) AND SPIN-OFF TECHNOLOGIES
FOR SOCIETAL AND INDUSTRIAL BENEFITS DEVELOPED BY DAE
21.1 The Committee understands that scientific Departments of Government of India have developed
a number of technologies that are ready for commercialisation. Department of Atomic Energy has
also developed many non-power applications and spin off technologies which have the potential to
serve the society in a number of ways for instance providing potable water, checking adulteration
in milk, keeping the environment clean and green and providing healthcare at affordable cost.
21.2 During its study visit to Mumbai in January 2017, the Committee visited the Bhabha Atomic
Research Centre on 21
st January, 2017 and held discussions on various aspects of scientific research
being undertaken by them. The Committee Members sought information regarding the BARC and
DAE’s fundamental contributions and findings in different fields. The Committee desired to know
about non-power applications and spin-off technologies developed for societal and industrial benefits.
In response thereto, it was informed that R&D in nuclear energy at BARC had not only generated
a comprehensive Indian Nuclear Power Programme but also has led to huge wealth of knowledge
in terms of large number of Non-Power Applications and spin-off technologies for societal and
industrial benefits. In response, the Department furnished the detailed list of significant Non-Power
applications and Spin-off technologies developed by various constituent units of Department.
(a) Nuclear Agriculture
In response to the Committee’s query about contribution to nuclear agriculture during
study visit to BARC in January, 2017 it was informed that the Department using
radiation and allied techniques had significantly contributed to release of high yielding
varieties in pulses and oilseeds over last 6 decades. BARC had also developed varieties
of Pigeon pea, Black gram, Soybean, Mustard and Green gram. In last 10 years, BARC
groundnut varieties had contributed to about 14.2% of National Breeders’ seed indent.
These varieties had become popular in groundnut growing States like Gujarat, Andhra
Pradesh, Odisha, Maharashtra, Rajasthan and Karnataka. BARC varieties in pulses like
mung bean, pigeon pea and blackgram had also played an important role in increasing
overall national productivity. The introduction of BARC pulse varieties suitable for rice
fallow cultivation had increased the use efficiency of agricultural fields.
(b) Nuclear Irradiation Technology for food preservation
During the study visit to BARC when the Committee desired to know about BARC’s
contribution to food preservation, it was informed that the incidence of diseases in
seeds and food-borne diseases could be reduced by food irradiation techniques. It could
also inhibit post-harvest sprouting in potatoes and onions – disinfect fruits and vegetables,
delay ripening in fruits, could eliminate out rightly the food-borne pathogens which
could be kept for a long time without refrigeration before substantial consumption. In
addition, the irradiation technology could be used for eliminating pests nuisance etc.
Feasibility of food irradiation for preservation has been studied for a number of agricultural
and food commodities for several years. There are several commodities cleared under
New Atomic Energy (Radiation Processing of Food & Allied Products) Rules 2012 in
Food Safety and Standards (Food Products Standards and Food Additives) Regulations,

38
2011. The major facility in the government sector catering to irradiation of fresh horticultural
produce is the KRUSHAK facility at Lasalgaon, Nashik district, Maharashtra, India.
(c) Healthcare & Industry
Bhabhatron-II is an isocentric, external beam radiation therapy machine designed for the
treatment of cancer patients developed by BARC. It uses radioactive cobalt-60 isotope
as the source of radiation. It is a computer-controlled system to deliver planned amount
of radiation exposure to the designated target safely and accurately. Following are the
features of Bhabhatron-II:
z Enhanced Safety (through automatic & full collimator closure);
z Asymmetric Collimation for improved conformity;
z Automatic patient setup for reliable and faster patient positioning;
z Motorized Wedge Filter for any desired does gradient;
z Battery back-up for regular operations even during power-cuts;
z High Source Capacity: 250 RMM (Roentgen/min. At one meter);
z Source to Axis Distance (SAD): 80 cm;
z Field Size: min. 0x0 (fully closed); max. 35 cmx35 cm;
z Extensive Clinical Trials by Tata Memorial Centre;
z Compliance to IEC Requirements (IFC601-1, IEC6060-2-11, MDD-93/42/EEC; and
z Approval by the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board, India.
(d) Board of Radiation and Isotope Technology (BRIT)
Board of Radiation and Isotope Technology (BRIT) has been established by the Department
to promote applications of radiation and radioisotopes for healthcare industry. Most of
the radioisotopes which are used, have been produced in research and power reactors
of the Department of Atomic Energy. Radioisotopes are formulated into a variety of
radiochemicals, radiopharmaceuticals, radiation sources and labelled compounds and supplied
to various institutions for various applications. Approximately, 1,00,000 consignments
are supplied every year.
Highlighting the medical and industrial applications, the Department stated that wide
variety of radioisotopes of different radiation characteristics are regularly produced at
the Dhruva reactor of BARC and are supplied to users for a wide ranges of medical
and industrial applications.
Apart from this, BRIT has been successful in propagating this technology. So far 14
such plants are operational in private sector, Co-operative and Semi Government sectors
under MoU with BRIT for the supply of source and other related works. These
plants are meant for processing of food and allied products and also for healthcare
products.

39
It was also informed that VECC is setting up a 30 MeV Medical Cyclotron for the
production of radio-isotopes for Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT)
imaging using Thalium 201, and Gallium 67. SPECT isotopes are currently being imported.
Technology has been developed at RRCAT for micro welding of high dose rate (Iridium
132) brachytherapy assemblies for cancer treatment. Development of compact and portable
optical spectroscopic systems (fluorescence, diffuse-reflectance and Raman scattering
based) for in-vivo screening of the cancer of oral cavity. The systems have been
deployed at Tata Memorial Hospital, Mumbai, Indore Cancer Foundation, Indore, and
Government Cancer Hospital, Indore for screening of patients.
(e) Water purification
Water and water purification includes purification with respect to microbiological
decontamination, arsenic removal, iron removal, de-fluoridation, salinity and hardness
removal. The technical know-how of these technologies have been transferred to several
private entrepreneurs on non-exclusive basis for commercial production and field deployment
of Health Care. Atomic Minerals Directorate (AMD) has successfully developed filters
for removal of uranium and arsenic from drinking water and other aqueous systems for
societal needs. As the invention is novel in nature and could find application in rural
areas, DAE-IPR Cell has recommended filing application in India for patenting the
invention.
In IGCAR, the Serium-89 isotope, used in palliative care applications, is being produced
in FBTR. The technology to remove fluoride from drinking water has been developed
and transferred to Tamil Nadu Water & Drainage Board, which is implemented in
Dharmapuri district of Tamil Nadu.
(f) Waste disposal
NISARGRUNA technology for disposal of solid biodegradable waste through degradation
has been commercialized and deployed on fairly large scale.
(g) Education
An excellent effort, in keeping with the mandate of the DAE to develop technology for
the betterment of the quality of life of the citizens of India, has been made in developing
software, called Mounisara, for automatic conversion of text to sign language for the
benefit of the hearing impaired.
As regards to human resource development in the country, various Associateship/Fellowship,
i.e., KSKRA/DGFS-Ph.D scheme have since been introduced in order to attract talent.
The number of active researchers in Science and Technology category is 198.
21.3 The Department has informed that scientists deliver lectures at schools, colleges, universities
and engineering colleges to acquaint students about latest scientific issues as well as career opportunities
in DAE. Students from across the country at all levels are encouraged to visit our centre and also
undertake short projects during summer/winter vacations.
21.4 The Committee appreciates Non-Power Applications and spin-off technologies developed
by Department of Atomic Energy for societal and industrial benefits in the field of agriculture,

40
food preservation, healthcare & industry, waste disposal and education, etc. It also appreciates
development of Mounisara software for the betterment of quality of life of the citizens of
India. In fact, technologies like Nisargruna can prove to be boon for the society at large
and industry which is grappling with the problem of disposal of sewage as well as solid waste
generated in metropolitan cities and small towns.
21.5 The Committee commends the Department for starting the seed production programme
at Vizag campus also and hopes that these efforts will benefit Odisha, Andhra Pradesh,
North-Eastern States and generate good quality seeds in eastern India.
21.6 While noting the development of Non-Power Applications and socially useful technologies,
the Committee is concerned with the slow pace at which these non-power applications and
socially useful technologies developed by the Department are trickling down to the targeted
groups in particular and society in general. This is primarily because Scientific Departments
have not made any proactive combined effort to create a dedicated agency and portal for
popularisation of socially useful technologies and other technologies ready for commercialisation.
However, DAE has made some good moves in this direction with Board of Radiation &
Isotope Technology. The Committee is aware the DAE has tied up with a private company,
CSIR tech for marketing of socially and industrially useful technology developed by the
Department.
21.7 On being asked about steps taken for popularisation of technology developed, the Department
has informed that so far Nisargruna technology has been transferred to 135 parties (till August
2016) and 100 plants of different capacities (250/500/1000/2000 kg per day) are operating to
process biodegradable waste in the country.
21.8 BARC has already installed one 2 MTPD Nisargruna biogas plant at Cochin shipyard. This has
been commissioned and functioning well. Currently a discussion is going on with the High Power
Committee of Sabarimala Temple Trust to install 6 Nisargruna biogas plants.
21.9 According to the Department, cost of Nisargruna plants vary depending on the capacity,
type of input waste, end use of gas generated, general topography of the place, location of
plant and user area, labour charges, etc. A general estimate for a 1 tonne per day plant is about
16-20 lakhs.
21.10  The Committee feels that the efficacy of non-power applications and spin off technologies
lies in their use on a large scale which requires propagation and popularisation of these
technologies.
21.11 In view of the above, the Committee recommends the Department and BARC to
execute their strategy to aggressively market its non-power applications and socially beneficial
technologies such as Nisargruna Biogas Plant for handling biodegradable wastes, Sludge
Hygienization Research Irradiation, Gamma radiation processing Plan, including its technology
on food preservation, molecular medicine and healthcare, through Board for Technology
Transfer & Collaboration Division and other possible mechanisms so that more and more
people get benefitted. AKRUTI Programme of the Department should also spread its activities
outside Maharashtra.

41
21.12 The Committee notes that the Department in collaboration with CSIR-Tech had signed
a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) for technology transfer and collaboration. However,
as per recent media reports, CSIR-tech has been closed down recently. The Committee,

21.13 Food preservation technology developed by BARC known as Trombay crop varieties

loans was `200.00 cr. each out of which NPCIL utilised the entire amount till 31
st January, 2017.
In response to the query of the Committee about enhancement of NPCIL’s IEBR component, it was
informed that NPCIL’s IEBR comprises borrowings, fund for R&D activities and Internal Accruals
of NPCIL. Borrowing for projects in respective year is considered based on approved financing
pattern prescribed in respective Financial Sanctions of the projects / schemes. Internal accruals are
arrived at residual value considering the borrowings.
23.7 The Department has informed that the IEBR realisation is based on the Capital Expenditure
during the period. The proposed IEBR reduction from the approved BE 2016-17 of ` 9222.00 crore
to ` 5082.00 crore in RE 2016-17 was on account of the proposed Capital Expenditure reduction
from ` 11494.00 crore in BE 2016-17 to ` 7136.00 crore in RE 2016-17. The proposed IEBR in
2017-18 of ` 5825.00 in BE 2017-18 was also consistent with the proposed capital expenditure of
` 8520.00 crore in BE 2017-18.
23.8 The Committee is happy to note that second unit of Kudankulam attained criticality
and synchronised with grid. The Committee also observes that the future plan of the
Department for capacity addition reveals that 6 indigenous and 5 new reactors with foreign
co-operation have been proposed. The Committee desires that NPCIL should expedite the
negotiation process with foreign collaborators in order to achieve total installed capacity of
about 600 MWe by 2024.
24. BHARATIYA NABHIKIYA VIDYUT NIGAM LTD. (BHA VINI)
24.1 As a part of 2
nd stage of Indian power program, 500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor
(PFBR) is being built for the demonstration of commercial scale power production. These reactors
produce more fuel than they consume and are essential for expansion and sustenance of Indian
nuclear power programme. PFBR will be fore-runner to a series of fast reactors being planned.
24.2 The Bharatiya Nabhikiya Vidyut Nigam Limited (BHA VINI), a Government of India Enterprise,
is a Public Limited Company set up with the objective of constructing and commissioning the first
500 MWe Fast Breeder Reactor (FBR) at Kalpakkam and establish subsequent Fast feeder Reactors
in the country.
24.3 The objective of BHA VINI is to plan, execute, and operate an integrated programme of Fast
Breeder Technology based Nuclear Power Stations for generating electricity on a commercial basis,

44
commencing with PFBR, symbolising commencement of the second stage of the Nuclear Power
Programme.
24.4 Performance of BHA VINI
Informing the Committee about physical progress the Department has informed that all construction
activities and total equipment erection and installation have been completed in Prototype Breeder
Reactor (PFBR). A number of mandatory pre-requisites tests viz. Integrated Leak Rate Test of
Reactor Containment building, commissioning of handling flasks for demonstrating the maintainability
of Primary Sodium Pumps, Pressure hold test of Reactor Assembly and Main Vessel, completion
of Pre-Service Inspection of 10% tubes of all the Steam Generators and segmental preheating of
sodium lines have been completed.
24.5 Presently, work is in progress for commencement of integrated pre-heating, towards which
the number of jobs pertaining to reductions of leaks in Reactor Containment Building and Reactor
assembly, trial testing of fuel handling systems and reactor protection system devices, augmentation
of supports for sodium piping, erection & installation of necessary piping for commencement of
nitrogen purging etc. are in progress.
24.6 The Department has informed that commissioning works were in full steam and all efforts
were being made to ensure that there were no further slippages owing to any errors in job-
scheduling so as to make the PFBR fully functional by October 2017.
24.7 The Committee finds that BHA VINI was allocated ` 20.00 crore for BE 2016-17 but by
January, 2017, it could not utilise the entire sum allocated to BHA VINI Project. However, this year
Budgetary support has been increased from ` 20.00 crore at BE 2016-17 to ` 50.00 crore at BE
2017-18. In response to the Committee’s query about substantial reduction in IEBR amount projected
for BE 2017-18 for BHA VINI, it was informed that the original plan was for 2x500 MWe Project.
However, it has been decided to go for 2x600 MWe. It was further decided to start this project
after completion of the first Project (PFBR). Since PFBR was getting delayed, consequently the
second project could not be started as planned.
24.8 In response to the Committee’s query about PFBR it was informed that PFBR is under
advanced stage of commissioning and the project was expected to be completed by October, 2017.
Although all construction activities, total equipment erection & installation have been completed in
PFBR, time scheduled for the First Approach to Criticality (FAC) followed by subsequent power
operation got shifted. This is primarily owing to augmentation of certain additional assessments and
checks on the installed equipment prior to commencement of their commissioning, which have
essentially emanated owing to both increased regulatory requirements and as a matter of abundant
caution.
24.9 In addition, as commissioning is under progress, occasional mismatches and design anomalies
in the system/ equipment between the prior assessments based on theoretical models and actual
observation are being noticed and appropriate rectification actions are undertaken. These anomalies
are essentially owing to First-Of-A-Kind (FOAK) design and engineering having no international
reporting/benchmarking.
24.10 During the meeting held on 13
th February, 2017, the Committee desired to know reasons
behind delay in commissioning of BHA VINI. The Secretary replied as under:

45
“Yes, we wanted to finish it last year. But as it is a new technology, from both the sides,
from the regulator’ s side and from the project side, we are going in a more conservative way.
We are trying to do tests and retests and then prove everything before we go ahead. So, what
I am expecting is that by October, 2017, we should be able to do it smoothly, and, Sir, I will
tell you today’ s status. Today, we have completed construction in all respects. All systems are
in operation and we are in the final phase of commissioning of this one. And this is a system
where instead of water cooling, we use sodium cooling and that works at about 600 degree
Celsius. That is a much higher temperature compared to what we see in other reactors or even
thermal power stations. This higher temperature causes some problem and there are some
concerns about that. Because of that, we are going in a very systematic way. Again, the
Atomic Energy Regulatory Board is going through all the steps. So, that also is making this
thing slower. The policy adopted is that we will be slow and steady but sure. That is the way
it is going on. And, you are right, Sir. Whatever uranium we get from the mines, only 0.7
per cent of it can be used because that is what is uranium-235. Whereas in this case, entire
uranium quantity can be used, which is hundred times or more, 140 times the total. That
means, if you get one kilogram of uranium from your mine, you can use 140 times compared
to what is available in other thermal reactors. Yes, it is a very important step. I am sure,
we will make it. We don’t have any technical problem. It is only a matter of time.”
The Secretary, Department of Atomic Energy further added
“Sir, uncertainty is not that much because we have a smaller reactor which is of 10 mw
capacity and it has been in operation for the last 25 years. The technology is same. As a
matter of fact, fuel is a little simpler here. But that is a much bigger reactor.  That is the
main difference. I cannot say that because of this reason it got delayed. It is a mix of
reasons. We are cautious at every step. That is the main reason for delay. If some problem
comes in rushing through it, then it will be questioned all over the world. It is not that just
India is responsible for this. I am sure something positive will happen. Please bear with us.
We are doing our best to make it work.”
Another senior scientist of Department of Atomic Energy added as under:
“Sir, I would just like to add to what the Secretary said just now. This technology was
designed at the Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research at Kalpakkam. It is a new
technology. As was rightly pointed out, it runs with sodium. Such programmes are either
stopped or delayed all over the world like France and Japan because of sodium leakage. We
are working with regulators to make sure that we get it right at the first step. Therefore, some
amount of caution has been built into it. We are a bit more cautious than other countries so
that we don’t fail once we get the reactor.”
24.11 The Committee feels that BHAVINI has an important role to play in bringing energy
security to the country. The Committee is of the view that if India has to successfully
realise the three stage Nuclear Energy Programme and thereby tap huge thorium reserves
of the country, Department has to make all out efforts for expediting the commissioning
and ramp up the capacity of Fast Breeder Reactor.
24.12 The Committee observes that there has been inordinate delay in commissioning of

46
Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor at Kalpakkam. As per the original schedule, the project was
to be commissioned in September, 2010 which was later rescheduled to September, 2014. The
goalpost was again shifted to September, 2016 and later on to October, 2017. The Committee
is disappointed to note that despite a Steering Committee headed by the Secretary himself
conducting regular meetings for monitoring the activities of PFBR, such meetings have not
yielded any concrete results as the completion schedule has been delayed considerably due
to various constraints resulting in delay in achieving criticality. While appreciating the
complexities involved in the project and extreme caution exercised by the Department, the
Committee hopes that the Department will expedite the remaining work so that the reactor
is commissioned by October, 2017 without any further dalay.
25. OUTREACH PROGRAMME
25.1 The Committee during its meeting held on 13
th February had observed that people of the
country including elected representatives are not aware of the excellent work in the field of Atomic
Energy being done by the Department which may be beneficial for a very big segment of the
society like farmers, fishermen, students, research scholars, etc.
25.2 The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department and its Public Sector
Units such as Uranium Corporation of India Limited, and Indian Rare Earths Limited
should prepare a comprehensive outreach programme with a calendar of events using social
media platforms, radio, television, etc. meant for students and general public and most
importantly for all the elected representatives right from district level i.e. Members of Zila
Panchayats, Legislative Assemblies and Councils and Members of Parliament.

and around its nuclear reactors. However, it still believes that a lot more needs to be done
for management of unfounded fears among the people and negative perception against
possible adverse fallouts of nuclear energy.
25.4 The Committee strongly feels that elected representatives can play an important role
in making their constituents aware of non-power applications and spin off technologies
developed by the Department and its Public Sector Units which have the potential to serve
the society in numerous ways and ultimately create a positive image about nuclear energy
in the mind of Indian public at large.

The Committee notes with satisfaction the achievements of the Department of Atomic
Energy in its 62 years of operation. In addition to its considerable achievements in the
nuclear power generation, the Department has also produced useful spin-off applications for
the benefit of the society and industry. Keeping in view the Department’s success, the
Committee is confident that the Department  will  be able to fulfil ten point vision  outlined
by NITI Aayog  for the Department. (Para 3.7)
TWELFTH FIVE YEAR PLAN OUTLAY
The Committee also finds that outlay of ````` 20,023 cr. could not be allocated to the
Department till financial year 2016-17. (Para 6.5)
PERFORMANCE IN TWELFTH FIVE YEAR PLAN
The Committee feels that this phenomenon of underutilization of allocated outlay is a
very serious matter towards which the Department needs to focus its attention in a more
professional manner and initiate concrete measures. Merely, reiterating that the Department
has already in place a robust monitoring mechanism would not do any good particularly in
view of the fact that underutilization of allocated budgetary resources has turned out to be
a recurring phenomenon. It becomes all the more imperative, as underutilization of allocated
resources provides the Ministry of Finance with an alibi to make less allocation in the next
year and also allows them to use it as a tool to reduce the approved BE outlay at the RE
Stage. (Para 7.8)
The Committee is of the considered view that the Department can justify its demand
for additional resources only when it is able to first utilise the entire resources allocated
to it. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of Atomic Energy must
make sincere efforts by way of meticulous planning, timely implementation and stricter
monitoring of schemes/projects. (Para 7.9)
The Committee also notes that the Department could not get allocations as per the
ratio of outlay approved for the Twelfth Five Year Plan. If the total approved outlay of
`````107186.73 cr. for the entire Twelfth Plan period be evenly distributed among the 5 Annual
Plans, the average allocation comes to approximately `````21437.34 cr. per Annual Plan. The
Committee finds that for 2016-17, the last year of the Plan period, the plan allocation at
BE level was less by `````5675.46 cr. compared to average allocation per year and if it is seen
in the perspective of the RE allocation, this gap further widens to `````11318.50 cr. which is
almost the half of the annual allocation during the Twelfth Plan period. The Committee is
aghast to find that for past five years, allocations for Externally Approved Projects could not
be finanalised by NITI Aayog/Ministry of Finance. The Committee taking a serious view in
this matter, feels that by doing this, Ministry of Finance has made a mockery of approved
outlay for the Twelfth Plan period. (Para 7.10)
47

48
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Finance must desist from
such practices and allocate budgetary resources in the Annual Plans in proportion due to the
Department or else the very purpose of long term allocations gets defeated. (Para 7.11)

On the overall analysis, the Committee finds that though non-scheme expenditure by
the Department is satisfactory but there is a considerable scope for improvement in the
Schemes because actual utilisation of funds in non-schemes is merely 56% by January,
2017. The Committee therefore is of the considered view that Department needs to improve
its fund utilisation. (Para 8.5)

under Industries & Minerals Sector and hopes that fund utilisation will see considerable
improvement in coming years. The Committee would like the Department to work proactively
to get clearances under projects in Industries & Minerals Sector. (Para 8.10)

strategic Department, should not be put at par with other Departments/Ministries. The

equipment from foreign countries, complex construction requires stage wise approval which
can take time the Department should also not be put under the restrictions like Instrument
of Service Rule for relocation of budget from one Head to other Head as equipments
involved in nuclear activities may be costlier than `````2.5 cr. However, the Department must also
desist from underutilising or surrendering funds without any solid reasoning. (Para 8.12)

to enable it to carry out its mandate smoothly and efficiently. Ministry of Finance/PMO/

for increase in outlay at RE stage favourably particularly under R&D Sector, fuel imports,

I, the Chairman of the Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and Forests, having been authorised
 by the Committee to present the report on its behalf, present this Third Report of the Committee. This Report deals with
 issues contained in the Annual Report of the Ministry of Environment & Forests for the year 1992-93.
 
2.         The Committee held in all four meetings on 7th, 8th, 9th June and 20th October, 1993 (Appendix). In the
 meeting held on 7th June, 1993, the representatives of the Ministry of Environment and Forests gave an overview of
 various activities of the Ministry. On 8th and 9th June, 1993 the Committee discussed in detail the activities of the
 Ministry.
 
3.         The Committee expresses its appreciation for the officials of the Ministry for their cooperation and making
 available the material whenever required by the Committee.
 
4.         The Committee considered and adopted the draft report at its meeting held on the 20th October, 1993.
 
NEW DELHI  
October 20, 1993
SYED SIBTEY RAZI
Chairman
Committee on Science and Technology,Environment and Forests

R E P O R T
 
GENERAL BACKGROUND
 
The very existence of the country and its all-round progress as we move into the future will be greatly dependent
 on sustainable development: It is, therefore, very vital that a check is exercised on the demands placed on the
 environment so as not to exceed the carrying capacity of the environment for the present as well as the future
 generations.
 
2.         We have in India, our own hoary traditions of environmental conservation which have inculcated in us a deep
 reverence for nature and an awareness of the age-old truth that all forms of life, be it human, animal or plant are inter-
woven and any damage to one may cause serious threat to the rest. The age-old traditions of environment protection and
 reverence to the mother nature have been given prominence in our national priorities as is evident from the
 constitutional provisions which enjoin upon all individuals a duty to protect and improve the natural environment,
 including forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife and to have compassion for living creatures. We have an impressive array of
 laws which aim at protecting and promoting environment and controlling pollution. Environment is also one of the
 priorities of our Planning.
 3.         However, it is being noticed that alongwith economic progress, pressure is steadily
 increasing on the environment and the natural resources; and this has reached in some cases
 alarming proportions. Environmental protection in the present scenario has become very
 vital for the prosperity of the country.
 4.         The Ministry of Environment and Forests, which is entrusted with the gigantic task of
 preserving the environment plants, promotes and coordinates environmental and forestry
 programmes. The main activities of the Ministry include conservation and survey of flora,
 fauna, forests and wildlife; prevention and control of pollution, undertaking programmes for on of degraded areas,
 protection of the environment and afforestation and re-generation of degraded areas, protection of the environment and
 promoting research related to these fields. These tasks are being fulfilled through environmental impact assessment,

 eco-regeneration, assistance to organisations implementing environmental and forestry research, extension, education
 and training to augment the requisite manpower, collection, collation, storage and dissemination of environmental
 information, and creation of awareness at the national level.
 
5.         With a view to assessing whether the Ministry is fulfilling its mandate effectively, the Committee decided to
 make an indepth study of the various aspects of the functioning of the Ministry by analysing its Annual Report for the
 year 1992-93.
 
6.         At the very outset, the Committee was appraised of the history of the creation of the Ministry of Environment
 and Forests and its functioning. The Committee was informed that conservation, study of and research on natural
 resources are the main thrust areas of the Ministry. To carry out this task, there are a number of institutions like
 Botanical Survey of India, Himalayan Institute of Environmental Development, National Museum of Natural History,
 Indian Council of Forestry Research and Education which are working under the Ministry. Raising environmental
 awareness among masses is an important task being performed by the Ministry. For this purpose, there is the National
 Environmental Awareness  Committee at the centre which is having a network with a number of non-governmental
 organisations all over the country. Besides this, there are 16 Environment Information Centres which have a potential
 for further expansion.
 
tonnes of fodder, calculated at a nominal rate of 50 paise per kg. comes to Rs. 12,500 crores per year. The Ministry was
 of the view that on a conservative estimate, the value of goods and services provided by the forests came around to
 approximately Rs. 26,500 crores per annum. The representative of the Ministry emphasised that the tremendous
 pressure on our forests was evidently unsustainable if appropriate amount of revenues generated from the forest areas
 was not reverted back towards the regeneration and renewal of the forest resources. It was felt that investment in this
 area should at least be 10% of the total benefit accrued. However, investment on such a scale is not available, the
 representative of the Ministry specifically elaborated upon the element of total neglect of this vital sector in all the Five
 Year plans, it was clarified that the allocation of the forestry sector for the 8th Five Year plan stood at Rs. 4082.00
 crores which was not more than 0.94% of the total allocation and showed perceptible decline when compared with
 percentage allocation of the forestry sector in the 7th Five Year Plan. Neglect could also be borne out by the fact that
 whereas organised energy sector comprising thermal, hydro-electrical and nuclear projects has at its disposal 25% of
 plan resources, rural energy had been given just one per cent.
 
13.       One heartening feature in the otherwise dismal scenario in the foresty sector is that India has been successful in
 attracting both multilateral and bilateral donors like the World Bank, Swedish International Development Authority
 (SIDA), Overseas Economic Corpora­tion Fund (OECF) (Japan), EEC and Official Development Assistance (ODA)
 (UK) to get assistance for this vital sector. This external assistance is likely to continue in future also. But due to
 inadequate funding by the Government of India, the externally aided forestry projects had failed to make the progress
 as laid down in the Approved Project Documents (APD). This created a very embarrassing position when the donor
 agencies found that the projects already sanctioned were falling behind .the schedule.
 
14.       As a result of the devaluation of the India rupee vis-a-vis all major foreign currencies, more rupee funds are
 needed to fully utilize the external assistance which has necessitated extension in the life of some projects. Due to
 financial constraints some State Governments are not able to make adequate provision in their budget for the project to
 utilize the aid. The Ministry informed that the State Governments are impressed upon from time to time to make
 adequate provision in the budget so as to utilise the entire aid for the project being implemented by them. The
 inadequate funding of the forest sector has resulted in (a) delayed implementation of the externally aided projects; (b)
 accretion to the foreign exchange reserves of the country from the soft loans and grants provided by the external donors
 is lower than it can be; and (c) the forest operations that were approved under the project cannot be undertaken as
 approved and the regeneration and renewal of the forest resources suffer.
 
15.       Employment generation is a core issue in our plan outlays. Tree planting activities offer a vast potential for

 employment generation. As per the estimates of the Ministry, afforestation and tree-plantation programmes have a
 wage component of nearly 70% which is much higher than the employment generation capabilities of other sectors of
 Indian economy. Other welcome feature of employment generation by this sector also alleviates hardships associated

 allocation of funds for afforestation and tree planting activities has now been done away-with in the Jawahar Rojgar
 Yojana. A positive action that has been taken in this area, however, is the creation of a joint management system for
 forests adjacent to villages. 13 States have already issued orders that wherever villagers are involved in planning
 preservation, protection, raising, management, etc. of new plantation, they should be provided free grass, fuel,
 medicinal plants, etc. Not only this, after harvesting 25 to 50% of the produce or the price would be kept at the disposal
 of the villagers.
 
16.       The representative also informed the Committee that enactment of the Forest (Conservation) act in 1980 has
 brought about a revolutionary change in the conservation of forests. Now, even State Governments can not arbitrarily
 transfer any forest land for non-forestry purpose. Not only this, it has now been made mandatory that in the event of
 transfer of forest land for any project, proportionate non-forest land would be transferred for forestry purpose in the
 state and the cost of afforestation would be borne by the project management. Despite all this forests are under heavy
 pressure. The Committee expressed its utmost concern over large scale deforestation involving illicit felling and
 removal of trees and arbitrary transfer of forest land for non-forestry purpose.
 
17.       The Committee suggested that the deforestation problem could be resolved to a great extent if a survey of
 villages where lot of land on river banks was lying vacant was conducted. Another suggestion was that wastelands in
 rural areas could be developed as energy farms, thereby providing much needed fuelwood to the villagers. The
 representative of the Ministry clarified that practice of putting wastelands to plantation of fuelwood and fodder species
 was already in vogue in all the States. The Committee also observed that a great stress has been laid on the plantation of
 babul and Eucalyptus trees, which are neither good for health nor are they fruit bearing and useful from ecological point
 of view. It was also enquired whether any alternative scheme for plantation of trees had been evolved. In this regard,
 particularly attention was drawn to the plantation of fruit bearing and other trees which increase the fertility of land.
 
18.       The Committee pointed out that Government sponsored tree plantation weeks are merely show schemes as no
 follow up action is taken to ensure care of the trees planted. The Committee also expressed concern over the
 effectiveness of afforestation programmes, especially wanted to know about the mechanism which exists for their
 monitoring and evaluation. The representatives of the Ministry replied that social forestry project sponsored by World
 Bank and other international agencies are continuously monitored not only by the Government but also by the donor
 agencies and also by the non-Governmental organisations. Mid-term evaluation of survival of sapplings planted under
 the national Social Forestry Project in Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh had also been
 conducted by the World Bank. It was reported to the Committee that among the developing countries India was
 considered as one of the most acceptable countries where donors feel that the funds were being utilised to the best
 advantage.
 
19.       The Committee was also informed that evaluation done in 36 districts shows that in 25 districts, survival
 percentage of saplings was more than 70% in 7 districts it was 60 to 70% and in four districts it was below 50%. In case
 of Government where the survival rate was low, the attention of the State Governments had been drawn and they had
 been advised to take precautionary measures. In this regard the Ministry also quoted a study undertaken by the Indian
 Institute of Public Opinion between 1983 and 1988 which revealed the survival rate of sapplings in some of the States
 as follows:-
 
 
State                                                                                    Survival percentage
 Karnataka                                                                                                     82.5%

20.       On the suggestion of the Committee that wherever possible wood could be substituted in order to preserve
 forests, the Ministry informed that already they have taken action in this regard. In housing sector and Railways, wood-
substitutes were already being used, it was also informed that in coordination with the departments of Animal
 Husbandry programme of silvipasture had also being taken up by which fodder would be grown outside forest land and
 people would be trained to stall-feed their animals instead of allowing them to graze. The Ministry was also involved in
 the distribution of smokeless chullahas and gobbar gas plants.
 
21.       The Indian Forest Act, 1927 is the main legislation which deals with management of forests by states. This Act
 has become quite old and needs proper updating, particularly in view of the conceptual changes that have been
 incorporated in the National Forest Policy of 1988. With a view to incorporating new concepts of forest management, a
 need 'is being felt to bring forward a revised and more comprehensive legislation. The Ministry of Environment and
 Forests is already seized of the matter and a draft revised legislation has been circulated among the State Governments
 for their comments. Comments on the draft of the revised legislation have been received from the States/Union
 Territories of Andaman and Nicobar lands, Arunachal Pradesh, Goa, Gujarat, Haryana, Himachal Pradesb, Kerala,
 Maharashtra, Mizoram, Punjab, Uttar Pradesh, Lakshdweep, Pondicherry and West Bengal. The remaining States have
 been requested to expedite their comments. The draft Bill would have to be reviewed in the light of the comments
 received from the State Governments as well as considered through the joint and collective consultation in the Inter-
State Council. The Committee feels that the urgency of the matter may be highlighted to the State Governments and the
 Union Territories and they may be requested to furnish their comments within a specified time-frame and in case they
 have no comments to offer that also may be informed to the Ministry; as this would obviate unnecessary delay in the
 matter of finalising a comprehensive Forest Act.
 
22.       The Committee is constrained to find that in spite of several laws, which aim at forest conservation and
 promoting afforestation, the forest areas are steadily undergoing various stages of degradation. The Committee feels
 that as almost every section of the society is closely linked, in one way or the other, with forests, responsibility of
 conservation and enhancement of forest areas should not be left with the Ministry of Environment and Forests alone.
 Instead, society at large should be fully involved in this task. The Committee is aware of the great contribution being
 made by non-governmental organisations and environmental experts in this area. There is, however, still enough scope
 for using official media to enlighten public about the far-reaching consequences of deforestation. To promote
 environ­mental education, programmes may be prepared in regional languages and shown frequently on television or
 broadcast on the radio, besides this, talks, plays, songs, etc. in local languages may be produced which can be broadcast
 or telecast to create interest and concern about environment among the general public. Special programmes may be
 devised for the rural masses in this regard.
 
23.       Forestry which is a vital sector of Indian economy has been unfortunately neglected in all the Five Year Plans.
 The Committee feels that allocation of Rs. 4082.00 crores for the forestry sector in the Eighth Five Year Plan, being
 0.94% of the total plan allocation is considerably low and, therefore, recommends that immediate steps should be taken
 for substantially increasing the allocation of funds for the forestry sector. At the same time, the Ministry should also
 explore the possibility of raising needed funds through the forestry sector which may be utilised again for regeneration
 of forests, protection of wildlife, etc. The Ministry should also ensure that there is no wastage of funds and the money
 sanctioned is actually used for increasing the forest cover. The Ministry shall have to be vigilant about illegal falling of
 trees and theft of forest wealth. All this will have a healthy effect on externally aided forestry projects as they could
 then be implemented efficiently and within prescribed time-frame by showing quick results.
24.       The forestry operations create assets for the village communities improve the water regime and contribute
 significantly to the rural development effort and for this reason, forestry operations must be seen as critical to the
 process of upgrading the rural economy and alleviating rural poverty. The Committee is,-therefore, of the view that
 employment generation programmes should invest a part of their allocation in afforestation and tree-planting activities
 to realise the vast employment potential of the forestry sector. Towards this end, the Committee recommends that at
 least 25% of funds be earmarked for afforestation and tree-planting activities under the Jawahar Rojgar Yojana and

25.       The Ministry informed that there arc 75 national parks and 421 sanctuaries. The Committee was also given an
 idea about the wildlife conservation which cover both flora and fauna. The present wildlife conservation strategy is
 two-pronged, on the one hand it aims at protecting species by legislation and on the other hand, it devotes itself to area
 conservation. The Wildlife Protection Act of 1972 is an important Act in this regard. As a result of an amendment to
 this Act in 1991, certain species of plants, .in addition to animals, were  brought under its ambit. In the species
 conservation programme, some mega projects like 'Project tiger', 'Project elephant' and 'Project Rhino' have been taken
 up besides, these mega projects, there are also projects for protecting minor species like 'Sibberian crane' and 'Pigmoy
 Hog' etc.
26.       On being asked about the floristic work done in different States of the country, the Ministry informed that
 whereas floristic work in many states is either continuing or has been completed. Bihar, Maharashtra, Orissa, Uttar
 Pradesh, Dadar and Nagar Haveli and Pondicherry were the States/Union Territories where work has yet to start.
27.       The Committee is happy to note that activities relating to identification, nomenclature, taxonomic description
 and enumeration of various species belonging to several families for Flora of Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland,
 Mizoram, Sikkim, Andaman and Nicobar Islands, South-Western ghat, Jammu and Kashmir and Madhya Pradesh ahs
 been completed. The Committee is, however, surprised to find that the floristic work is yet to begin in some of the big
 states. The Committee hopes that work in the remaining states/Union Territaries would also begin shortly and the
 Ministry would make concerted efforts in this direction.
28.       The Committee noted that during the 7th Five Year Plan the Ministry had provided assistance to 150 sanctuaries
 and national parks under the scheme 'Development of National Parks and Sanctuaries'. 24 States got assistance for
 control of poaching. Three new tiger reserves were notified and brought under the purview of the Project Tiger
 Scheme.- In the 8th Five Year Plan two schemes namely, control of Poaching and Illegal Trade in Wildlife and
 Conservation of Rhinos in Assam have been transferred to States.
29.       Incidents of poaching in national parks and sanctuaries are often reported in the newspapers. The Committee
 feels that it is a serious crime and effective steps should be taken at the level of Ministry to curb this illegal practice.
 The Ministry cannot remain a silent spectator to the illegal trade in wildlife on the ground that national parks and
 sanctuaries are under the control of respective State Governments. The Committee is of the firm view that an
 institutional system should be devised whereby state Governments may be asked periodically to furnish reports
 mentioning cases of illegal poaching in the national parks and sanctuaries reported to them or noticed by them and the
 action taken against guilty persons.
Bio-sphere Reserves
30.       Biosphere Reserves are, multipurpose protected areas to preserve genetic diversity in representative ecosystems.
 Since the launching of the programme, the following seven Bio­sphere Reserves have been set up:
Nilgiri (Karnataka, Kerala & Tamil Nadu)
Nanda Devi (Uttar Pradesh)
Norket (Meghalaya)

Gulf of Mannar (Tamil Nadu)
Manas (Assam)
Sunderbans (West Bengal)
 
31.       The Ministry informed that the National Committee on Bio-sphere Reserves which was set up in December,
 1992 takes an integrated approach for implementation, monitoring and evaluation of the Bio-sphere Reserves
 Programme, Financial assistance for the current financial year for Bio-sphere Reserves namely, Noket, the Great
 Nicobar, Nanda Devi Sunderbans, Gulf of Mannar, Nilgiri has been allocated. However, in respect of manas
 Bio­sphere Reserve possibility of opening of bi-national Bio-sphere Reserve between India and Bhutan is being
 explored.

 policy makers as well as for those conducting research in the area of management and conservation of bio-diversity.
National Fund for Afforestation and Wastelands Development
34. According to the Ministry the National Fund for Afforestation and Wastelands Development was set up on the 17th,
 July, 1990, to achieve the objective of involving all sections of society and mobilising resources of individuals as well
 as organisations, both corporate and non-corporate in the task of wastelands development. On being asked about the
 corpus of the fund, the Committee was informed that a sum of Rs.11,01,85 is presently available in the fund which has
 to be spent on projects submitted by Government Departments/Trusts/Public Sector Undertakings/Local
 Bodies/Cooperatives/Companies. The Committee was also informed that wide publicity was given about the setting up
 of Fund within the country and outside also.
35.       The Committee feels that the Ministry has not given adequate publicity to the setting up of the Fund, as no
 project proposals have been received by the Ministry so far. Besides, the money lying in the Fund in not sufficient to
 achieve afforestation and Wastelands development in an effective manner. In order to involve individuals and
 organisations, more publicity should be given to the programme not only to attract money for the Fund but also to
 disburse money to the Government Departments, Cooperatives, local bodies etc. who may submit sound proposals for
 the afforestation and wastelands development.
Aerial Seeding
36.       The Committee felt that the plantation on mountain tops has generally remained neglected which could be
 effectively tackled by aerial seeding. The Ministry informed the Committee that a centrally sponsored scheme has been
 tried in the past in the States of West Bengal, Madhya Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Rajasthan. However, the
 Ministry is not sure about the cost effectiveness and usefulness of aerial seeding. The Committee feels that if aerial
 seeding is found to be cost-effective, then more areas may be identified for the purpose.
Housing and Construction activities by Private colonisers in hill areas
37.       The Committee highlighted the recent phenomenon of colonizers moving towards hilly areas and promoting
 housing activities there. While everybody wants to enjoy the salubrious climate of the hills but then it is also to be seen
 that the ecology of the hills is not disturbed or destroyed. If ecological imbalance is caused in hilly areas, it will have
 serious repercussions even for those who are living in plains. But the Ministry has not devised any method to check or
 control these colonizers from moving towards hills. The Committee feels that the Ministry of Environment and Forests
 should take up this matter with States having hilly terrains, particularly those where Himalayan ranges lie and impress
 upon the state Governments that there should be strict check on the construction activity promoted by the private
 colonizers for the purpose of making huge profit.
Prevention and Control of Pollution
38.       Pollution control is another thrust area identified by the Ministry of Environment and Forests. There are various
 policies and programmes relating to abatement and control of pollution which are administered by the Ministry. There
 also exist many schemes which are administered either directly by the Central Pollution control Board or through the
 State Boards. The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) is the principal agency which advises the Ministry on
 technical matters in formulating standards with regard to water and air pollution and other related areas. It also

 functions as an enabling organisation helping the state Pollution Control Boards to perform their roles in an effective
 manner. This is done by having a regular inter-action with State Pollution Control Boards.
39.       The Committee drew the attention to an announcement made in the recently concluded Conference of State
 Ministers of Small Scale Industries whereby henceforth clearance certificate for compliance with existing pollution
 control laws was not required for small scale industries and wanted to know the exact position in the matter. The
 Ministry clarified that in view of a large number of representations received from small scale industries, it has been

 of small scale industries may have simply to submit a forms to the State Pollution Control Boards. Further, was no need
 for the industry to obtain periodic renewal of consent till such time as the unit modified its process itself. However,
 random checks could always be conducted by the State Pollution Control Boards. In order to help small scale
 industries, government is implementing a scheme for providing assistance for promoting combined facilities for
 treatment of effluent and solid wastes generated in clusters of small scale units.
 
40.       Task forces have been set up by the CPCB on air pollution control in urban areas. Despite all these measures
 initiated by the Ministry, the Committee was of the view that the pollution load is increasing day by day. The Ministry
 had admitted itself that the average rate of growth in the industrial sector during the Seventh Five Year Plan was 8.87%
 with the liberatisation of industrial policy the growth rate is expected to be significantly higher. This would naturally
 lead to the increased pollution load. While the Committee notes that the Ministry has issued instruction that industries
 that came into operation after 16.5.1981 were to comply with standards by 31.12.1993, the control of pollution, in fact,
 calls for stringent measures. The Ministry should very closely monitor the industries in order to make them conform to
 the standards laid down by the target date.
41.       The Committee recommends that the Central Pollution Control Boards (CPCB) should coordinate with the State
 Pollution Control Boards in order to bring out an updated version of the inventory of all polluting industries, as the
 inventory prepared in 1984 has become outdated.
42.       The Committee also pointed out that the Effluent Treatment/Plant located at Najafgarh is not functioning
 properly and steps may be taken to set it in order. The Ministry informed the Committee that it is taking up the matter
 with the concerned authorities.
43.       The representatives of the Ministry were asked to clarify the specific actions taken toward prevention, control
 and abatement of air pollution after the promulgation of the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981. The
 Committee was informed that a number of actions have been taken in this regard. Guidelines have been issued for
 assessing the emissions and effluents based on the quantum of production. Guidelines have also been issued to
 encourage the utilisation of waste as a resource, wherever it is possible. Steps have also been taken to curb automobile
 pollution. Gross and mass emission standards for all types of vehicle have been notified under the Motor Vehicle Rules,
 1989.
44.       Vehicular traffic is, in fact, one of the major sources of air pollution in cities, particularly in those spots which
 have high traffic density. In Delhi itself vehicular exhaust causes air pollution by more than 60%. The Department of
 Transport of the Delhi Administration has formulated a detailed schemes in July, 1990 for certification of pollution
 standards of private vehicles registered in Delhi. The Government has also started a programme of running battery
 operated buses so as to minimise vehicular pollution. DTC has made a comprehensive action plan to reduce pollution
 and control smoke emission from its buses. This action plan consists of (a) reducing smoke emission by tuning
 vehicles/engines (b) acquiring buses for replacement of over-aged buses from active fleet (c) reducing overloading (d)
 introducing buses with fuel conservative engines (e) equipping the units with smoke meters for monitoring the smoke
 levels of the fleet in the unit, But it appears that this plan is hardly put to use. The Committee feels that the owner of
 private vehicles which pollute the air should be heavily fined and disincentives should be instituted for the owner of
 such vehicles. In congested areas where pollution load is already very high use of battery operated public transport be
 introduced. People may be encouraged to car-pooling and public transport systems with proper check on vehicular
 emission be promoted. Wherever possible pathways may be laid which can be used safely by the pedestrians and for
 those using cycles.

45.       The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Environment and Forests should issue instruction to all
 Government Departments including the Ministry of Defence, that the fleet of vehicles maintained by them should fully
 conform to the pollution control norms. And in this regard a responsible officer in the Ministries and Government
 offices may periodically conduct surprise checks in this regard.
46.       The Committee hopes that prescribed emission standards would be strictly adhered to by all concerned. The
 Committee finds that one of the actions taken is to persuade the industries to comply with the consent requirements of
 the State Pollution Control Boards within the stipulated period. The Committee feels that only persuasive action would
 not be effective and if necessary, punitive measures may also be involved.
47.       The Committee is happy to find that noise has been included as pollutant under the Air (Prevention and Control
 of Pollution) Amendment Act, 1987 and standards for ambient noise, automobile noise and noise from domestic
 appliances have been notified too. There also exists a code of practice for the abatement and control of noise pollution
 from public address system, aircraft operations, railway operations, construction activities and bursting of crackers. The
 Committee, however, feels that in spite of there being so many provisions, noise pollution from public address system
 and domestic appliances continues unabated. No doubt, due thought has been given to all the methods/actions required
 for curbing noise pollution in the legislative framework, but what is sadly lacking is its effective and forceful
 application. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the laws enacted for curbing the noise pollution should be
 strictly enforced.
48.       The Committee wanted to know about the continuous air quality monitoring stations which are functioning in
 the country. The Ministry informed that the two air monitoring stations are already in operation and data are regularly
 collected from these stations. There was a programme to set up a third monitoring station also but the equipment got
 damaged while importing it. It is being repaired to make it functional. The Committee feels that in view of the
 constantly increasing pollution in the country a feasibility study for the setting up of more such monitoring stations be
 carried out and some more monitoring stations be set up.
State Pollution Control Boards
49.       The Committee pointed out that while it is the responsibility of the State Pollution Control Boards to check
 pollution in their respective States, in most of the cases proper monitoring is not done and many complaints are made
 against State Pollution Control Boards. Admitting that the Ministry has been receiving complaints about inadequate,
 monitoring, the secretary of the Ministry informed that State Boards were asked to take suitable action in such matters.
 Besides that in serious cases or where complaints are being received very often the Ministry directly intervenes and
 asks the Central Pollution Control Board to look into them. If the complaints of corruption are received against the
 personnel of the Boards, the Government takes up these matters with the State Departments of Environment. The
 Committee, however, feels that State Pollution Control Boards should be activised. Their work should be streamlined
 and they should be strengthened. State Pollution Control Boards which carry out the policies laid down by the CPCB
 are flooded with various kinds of litigation. The Committee suggests that the CPCB may render all possible help to the
 State Boards for the settlement of the cases.
Ganga Action Plan and National River Action Plan
50.       Over the years, the process of development, unplanned growth of towns on the banks of the rivers and
 industrialisation which has spread over the vast area have been the prime factors behind the rising pollution in the
 rivers. In 1985, a programme for cleaning up the river Ganga in the States of U.P., Bihar and West Bengal was
 launched. In the first phase, it has been decided to deal with the pollution problems caused by discharge of municipal
 sewage into the river, lack of proper individual and community toilets and throwing of the unburnt or half burnt bodies
 in the river.
Out of 261 schemes under the Ganga Action Plan (GAP), 208 schemes coming under various categories had
 been completed by 30th April, 1993. Of the remaining 53 on-going schemes, 44 schemes are targeted to be completed
 by 1993-94, 8 more are likely to be completed by 1994-95. One schemes may spillover beyond this period. The State
 Govern­ments have been asked to ensure expeditious implementation of these schemes.
52.       To assess the impact of GAP schemes in terms of water quality improvement, 27 selected locations (20 on the
 mainstream of Ganga and 7 on the tributaries) are being monitored since 1986, 42 parameters namely; physio-chemical
 and bacteriological (25), heavy metals and pesticides (17) are monitored in this exercise.

 Varanasi, Patna and Uluberia towns where the pollution abatement schemes, wholly or in part, have been

 the Ministry Stated as follows:--

 not been completed. Out of 147 million litres which are generated in Varanasi, 125 have been

 monitoring, there will be some improvement in water quality. In Allahabad, the picture is not still good
 because for the 110 million litres generated the treatment plant is not complete."
55.       Attention of the Ministry was drawn to various small scale industries and tanneries which are discharging most
 of the effluents into the river Ganga at Kanpur. In Unnao also tanneries are causing lot of pollution. To tackle this
 situation the Secretary informed that the Ministry is trying to enforce the provisions of the law relating to pollution
 control. In Kanpur, the small scale industries and tanneries have already set up a common effluent treatment plant. In
 Unnao also they are setting up the Unnao Tannery Pollution Control Company with the assistance of the Industrial
 Bank of India. Effort is also being made to take up the highly polluting small scale industries and tanneries as part of
 the Ganga Action Plan.
56.       The Committee noted the work so far done in cleaning up of the river Ganga. The Committee is of the opinion
 that in the cleaning up operation of the rivers there should be greater community involvement. Unless people are taught
 the methods as to how they can keep their rivers clean, efforts of the Government will not achieve the desired success.
 The Committee strongly recommends that the cleaning up of the river Ganga in Kanpur, Allahabad and Varanasi
 should be attended to with all earnestness. Adverse effects of continued unhygienic practices on the banks of the river
 such as bank side defecation, Cattle wallowing, cloth washing, carcass and solid waste dumping, ritual offerings and
 mass bathing should be highlighted through official media so that there is a gradual decrease in such practices. The
 Committee hopes that with the change in the attitude of people, the pace of which is, of course, slow, the infrastructure
 created like electric crematoria, individual and community toilets, etc. would be utilised to a greater extent and the
 quality of water of the river Ganga will improve.
57.       The Committee was informed that in order to cleanse other rivers from pollution a National River Action Plan
 has been proposed. Under this plan pollution abatement measures would be initiated in various grossly polluted
 stretches of major  rivers in the country. Based on the present studies of grossly polluted stretches, the river Ganga,
 Yamuna, Damodar, Gomti, Hindon, Sabarmati, Sutlej, Subarnarekh, Godavari, Krishna, Kali, Khan, Shipra, Baitarni,
 Badra, Brahmani, Tunga, Cauvery, Tapti, Narmada and Betwa have been covered.
58.       As regards river basin studies the Committee was informed that out of the 14 major rivers in respect of which
 basin studies have been taken up by the Central Pollution Control Board in consultation with the State Pollution Control
 Boards, studies for 5 rivers have been completed and reports prepared. These are Ganga (Main), Ganga (Yamuna Sub-
basin), Sabarmati, Subarnarekha, Krishna and Brahmani-Baitarani. In case of three rivers namely, Brahmaputra, Indus
 (J&K portion) and Pennar, the studies have yet to commence. For rest of the rivers studies are at different stages of
 completion. The Committee feels that this work should be completed and reports published at an early date.
Hazardous Substances Management
59.       As a sequel to the Bhopal Gas Tragedy in 1984, the Government of India enacted the Environment (Protection)
 Act, 1986. Under the Act the responsibility in laying down the procedure and safeguards for handling of hazardous
 substances and prevention of accidents was entrusted to the Ministry of Environment and Forests. To discharge this
 responsibility a separate division called Hazardous Substance Management Division has been functioning in the
 Ministry. The Committee was informed that the first priority of the Ministry is the prevention of accidents for which the
 Ministry has developed its on site Management Plan for the industries. Under this Plan training is imparted to the
 workers employed in hazardous industries so that the risk of accident is minimal. In addition, the Ministry also
 undertakes risk assessment within these industries in order to find out the root cause of the accident, in case, any
 accident occurs. The Ministry does not permit setting up of industry dealing with hazardous substance unless it submits
 to the Ministry a safety report. If by any chance an accident takes place, the Ministry takes immediate remedial
 measures to mitigate the sufferings caused by the disaster. The Ministry has provided the State Governments

 Import of Hazardous Chemicals. Rules are inspected regularly by the concerned authorities. On-site plans are prepared
 by the industrial units whereas preparation of off-site emergency plan is the responsibility of the District Collector. The

 rules relating to the handling of bio-medical wastes may also be finalised with urgency and for this the Ministries and
 organisations which have been consulted by the Ministry of Environment and Forests may be asked to expedite their
 comments.
Sardar Sarovar Project

 Project commissioned by the World Bank namely, that detailed assessment of social, human and environmental impacts

 commenced as yet or not.

 recommendation made by the World Bank for carrying out realistic Environmental Impact Assessment of the Sardar
 Sarovar Project. The question of environmental impact assessment is not merely a technical requirement. In fact, it
 involves a broader question of human welfare and affects society in a direct manner. Before work any project
 commences, the project authorities should see to it that proper plans are chalked out for the rehabilitation of the oustees.
 The Committee is surprised to note that absence of these recommended studies did not deter the Government from
 going ahead with the project. The Committee feels that the independent review of the Sardar Sarovar Project
 commissioned by the World Bank should have been accorded due importance. The Committee is pained to note that in

Tehri Dam Project
65.       As regards the Tehri Dam Project the Committee enquired whether environmental impact assessment of the
 Tehri Dam Project was done before initiating the Project. The representative of the Ministry clarified that this project
 was initiated at a time when there existed no requirement for carrying out such studies. It was only in 1980 that an
 evaluation of the environmental impact assessment was ordered by the then Prime Minister. However, report in this
 regard could be submitted only in 1986. As an outcome of the Report, it was, however, decided in October 1986 that
 the Tehri Dam Project should be finally abandoned A query was then made about further scientific studies on micro-
level seismicity and actual testing on the design for accellerogram of Gazli Earthquake as recommended by a High-
Level Committee of Experts constituted by the Department of Mines. It was informed that this study has not yet been
 taken up. Expressing the concern about environmental damage caused by the Tehri Dam, the Committee enquired
 whether ecological balance around the areas has been restored. The representative admitted that the environmental
 damage caused by the Tehri Dam would be manifested over a very large area including the catchment, dam-site and the
 command. On being pointed out by the Committee that comprehensive studies are required to be taken up for evolving
 requisite environmental action plans, the representative  submitted that these Action Plans were still under formulation.
 Action has only been taken up for catchment Area Treatment, Rehabilitation of oustees and Compensatory
 Afforestation.

 1986. However, the scientific studies as stipulated by the High Level Committee of Experts to be carried out have not
 yet been taken up through the Department of Mines. The Committee expresses its serious concern over this inordinate
 delay and recommends that these studies should begin without any further delay. The Committee fails to understand the
 factors behind non-formulation of all the requisite Environmental Action Plans which were essential for mitigating
 adverse implication of environmental changes cause by the Tehri Dam Project and hopes that this sensitive issue would
 be accorded top priority by the Ministry.
Environmental Statement and Audit

 (Protection) Act, 1986 making environmental statement mandatory has been issued which requires all industries

 implemented with the cooperation of various industrial associations. Assistance is also being given to the Development
 Commissioner, small scale industries for major awareness programmes covering all states. The Committee has also
 learnt that the Ministry is bringing out a booklet giving details as to how environmental audit should be conducted. The

 Companies Act 1956 to include the Environmental Statement in the Annual Reports of the Companies. The Committee
 was also informed that the environment impact assessment work shops are being organised for training personnels from
 the Central and State Governments and their agencies in the field of environmental impact assessment (EIA). It is
 proposed to strengthen a few centres in the country with regard to EIA and also continue the programme. The
 Committee feels that techniques of environmental audit should also be incorporated in such training programmes.

Effect of Pollution on the Taj Mahal

 Agra. The Committee was informed that steps have been taken to improve the environment so that the Taj Mahal is not
 affected by the pollution in the air. The area around the Taj Mahal has been delimited and in the 'non-development

 up which are non-polluting. The problem posed by the Mathura Oil Refinery is also being looked into. The actual
 problem is being caused in Agra by the foundries and vehicular pollution. The Mathura Oil Refinery and the Railways

 caused by the pollution. The Taj Mahal forms part of our national heritage. It is one of the most beautiful monuments in
 the world. The Committee strongly recommends that concerted efforts should be made to protect this monument from
 environmental pollution. The Committee is not satisfied with the situation as it obtains today and desires that a time-
bound action plan for the protection and restoration of the Taj Mahal be prepared.
